items._ogDesc: Global shares were mixed and oil prices retreated Monday, falling sharply on renewed hopes for progress in diplomatic efforts between the U.S. and Iran.
items.body:
HONG KONG — Global shares were mixed and oil prices retreated Monday, falling sharply on renewed hopes for progress in diplomatic efforts between the U.S. and Iran.

U.S. futures advanced after U.S. stocks fell Friday to their worst day since June as investors dumped artificial intelligence-related and other technology stocks.

In early European trading, Britain’s FTSE 100 edged down 0.1 per cent to 10,721.94. Germany’s DAX climbed 0.1 per cent to 25,849.98, while the CAC 40 in Paris added 0.1 per cent to 7,975.87.

In Asia, Japan’s Nikkei 225 gave up early gains, slipping 0.3 per cent to 63,081.86 as some major technology companies fell.

Shares of OpenAI investor SoftBank Group dropped 1.6 per cent. Japanese memory chipmaker Kioxia Holdings plunged 15.8 per cent as its earnings forecasts disappointed some analysts and investors.

South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index rose 2.2 per cent to 5,859.08. Samsung Electronics added 1.8 per cent, while memory chipmaker SK Hynix jumped 3.8 per cent.

Technology stocks have wavered as investors fret that the AI buildup may prove to be a bubble.

Apple is due to report its latest earnings results later in the day. Last week, earnings reports from Google parent Alphabet Inc. and Amazon rattled markets and raised fresh questions over whether their massive AI-related spending will bring profitable returns as quickly as hoped.

While recent developments do not necessarily mean that the AI boom is beginning to unravel, the debate is entering another phase, Sunil Tirumalai at UBS Global Research wrote in a recent note.

Investors have become “distinctly more nervous about a handful of companies with weaker balance sheets or bigger financial commitments,” he said, rather than the technology sector as a whole.

“Some cracks have appeared,” said Tirumalai. “Increasingly, the question will be whether all the money being spent on it can generate adequate financial returns.”

Over the past month, the Nikkei 225 has fallen more than seven per cent and the Kospi dropped more than 16 per cent.

Taiwan’s Taiex was 0.7 per cent lower, with leading chipmaker TSMC, or Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., shedding 1.7 per cent.

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng gained 0.4 per cent to 23,393.32. The Shanghai Composite index was up 1.1 per cent to 3,638.03, despite China reporting over the weekend that its factory activity returned to contractionary territory in October.

China’s central bank and its securities regulatory body met with financial institutions to discuss ways to support the markets, according to Chinese media reports. The Shanghai Composite index has fallen more than eight per cent since the beginning of this year and nearly 15 per cent from its highest level in the past year.

The People’s Bank of China said Monday that around 100 billion yuan (US$15 billion) would be deployed under a new swap facility that will provide dozens of financial firms more liquidity that can then be used to invest in the market.

In Australia, the S&P/ASX 200 lost 0.6 per cent to 8,856.50.

India’s Sensex rose one per cent.

On Friday, Wall Street’s benchmark S&P 500 fell 1.8 per cent and the technology-heavy Nasdaq composite declined 2.9 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average slid 1.1 per cent.

Investors are watching for the outcome of Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections. Voters across the political spectrum have shown increasing concerns about AI and data centres, along with inflation and other key issues.

Oil prices dropped more than two per cent early Monday, with Brent crude, the international standard, down 3.9 per cent to $109.01 per barrel. Still, that’s much higher than the roughly $72 a barrel level in late February before the war.

Benchmark U.S. crude gave up 4.1 per cent, to $99.82 a barrel.

Uncertainties surrounding the situation in the Middle East continued to pressure global oil supplies, particularly over the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for global oil transport.

Iran’s top diplomat said in an interview shared on his Telegram channel over the weekend that Iranian negotiators were in Qatar for talks on a proposal that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the U.S. meets several conditions. However, he said no direct talks were being held with the U.S.

The final outcome of the diplomatic efforts to avoid a return to all-out war depends on answers provided by the United States to the “Iranian questions,” he said.

In other dealings early Monday, the U.S. dollar rose to 157.64 Japanese yen from 157.49 yen. The euro was trading at $1.1236, up from $1.1160.

Chan Ho-him, The Associated Press

items.title: Parents cheer, businesses brace as Western Canada ditches the time change
items.description: Jenn Irwin-Greer never looked forward to the routine gong show at her Edmonton dayhome business that came with the twice-annual time change as children struggled to adjust to a new pattern.

items._ogDesc: Jenn Irwin-Greer never looked forward to the routine gong show at her Edmonton dayhome business that came with the twice-annual time change as children struggled to adjust to a new pattern.
items.body:
Jenn Irwin-Greer never looked forward to the routine gong show at her Edmonton dayhome business that came with the twice-annual time change as children struggled to adjust to a new pattern.

“(Children) show up a little bit irritable, as we all do when we’re tired,” she said. “Nap times get thrown out of whack.”

She’s hopeful things will be a little bit easier this year.

Canadians woke up Sunday to a new time zone map after British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba, northwestern Ontario and the Northwest Territories opted to stay on daylight time year-round rather than have clocks fall back one hour.

Saskatchewan already doesn’t adjust its clocks.

At a recreation centre in Edmonton’s south end on Sunday, some parents said not having to adjust their children’s sleep schedule felt refreshing.

“I’m going to be honest, I do kind of like it,” said Amanda Petrie after her seven-year-old son’s hockey game. “It’s just easier with kids when you don’t have to adjust their schedule.”

Siva Sivabalan, another resident, said he felt the Alberta government had made the right call by not changing the time.

“I rather have more daylight in the evening time rather than the morning,” he said as his daughter played nearby.

“Especially the November time change, I just didn’t like it at all.”

In Calgary, hairstylist Jordan Janovcik said he feels anxious about the work week ahead.

He said he spent the entire summer double- and sometimes triple-checking with clients to make sure they knew Alberta was not falling back.

Hairstylists like him have busy but by-the-book schedules, and missed appointments or delays could mean lost time and money.

“I am really concerned for this week,” he said in a phone interview.

“I think this is going to be really hard for a lot of businesses.”

Technology experts have said the change could cause problems for scheduling systems and older computer software.

Online, some Canadians reported Sunday that their cellphones displayed the incorrect time.

A statement from Telus says the issue is related to how some phones update their time zone information, rather than the service provider.

“Customers experiencing this issue can check their phone’s settings to ensure that ‘set time zone automatically’ is selected, then restart their phone to help apply any available time zone updates,” the company says.

A Rogers spokesperson said the company experienced no issues with its network, and referred questions to an industry group that posted instructions for updating phones and tablets.

In the skies, Air Canada said Sunday its operations were normal, noting that all flights use the internationally recognized time standard and that time changes are managed using established industry data sources.

Tech giant Google responded to an inquiry about how new time zones are affecting its services by linking to a blog post with instructions on how to make sure devices and services stay on schedule.

“From morning alarms to critical calendar invites, we know how much you rely on your devices to stay organized and on time,” the post said.

“Our teams are working to ensure these updates reach all Canadian users as quickly as possible.”

Back in Edmonton, Irwin-Greer said she’s curious how no time change might affect life on the Prairies.

She noted darker mornings in the months ahead and whether they would affect commutes for students and workers.

“I don’t love that it’s going to be darker for longer when the kids are going to school,” she said. “My teenage son is not overly worried about it, but it is a little bit concerning when they’re trying to travel.

“Crossing the street and it’s hard enough for traffic to see, so hopefully there are not more accidents.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 2, 2026.

With files from Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman in Montreal

Ashley Joannou and Fakiha Baig, The Canadian Press

items.body:
OTTAWA – Boosting trade and attracting investment will be top priorities for Prime Minister Mark Carney this week as he travels to St. John’s, Antigua and Barbuda to take part in the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM), from Nov. 2 to 4.

This year’s theme for the biennial meeting is “Accelerating Partnerships and Investment for a Prosperous Commonwealth.”

The government says Canada is looking to deepen its partnerships within the Commonwealth with the goal of creating new economic opportunities.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

“In a more dangerous and divided world, Canada is drawing closer to our Commonwealth partners,” said the prime minister in a statement.

“We are turning our shared values into shared strength – expanding trade and deepening climate co-operation to build a safer, more prosperous future for our peoples.”

Canada is the Commonwealth’s second-largest financial contributor and third largest economy, behind only India and the United Kingdon.

His Majesty King Charles III, who is head of the Commonwealth, along with Queen Camilla are expected to attend this year’s event on the small Caribbean Island. King Charles III is set to address the opening ceremony on Tuesday.

In the leadup to the summit, the Commonwealth Secretariat unveiled an investment platform with over 60 “high impact” projects submitted by 20 developing commonwealth countries looking for funding.

The list of “investment-ready projects” is said to represent over $30 billion.

Canada has over $100 billion in trade with Commonwealth countries

A senior government official speaking with reporters on background during a technical briefing for the trip highlighted the economic potential for Canada within the Commonwealth.

“He (the prime minister) has a tremendous opportunity to engage with many other leaders to advance some of the Canadian government priorities, from deepening partnerships to looking at ways to enhance trade and investment ties and to advance trade diversification,” the official said.

The official also pointed to a focus at this year’s summit on delivering results.

“What we can do to advance trade and investment within the Commonwealth countries, especially with smaller countries, to enhance inclusive and sustainable economic development.”

Officials say the prime minister’s discussions with other leaders are expected to address deepening partnership, trade diversification, and investment ties, including with smaller Commonwealth countries.

During the summit the prime minister has also been invited by King Charles III to attend a ceremony for new heads of government to welcome them into the Commonwealth.

‘This is a test’: International trade expert

CTV News spoke with international trade lawyer Barry Appleton about Carney’s upcoming trip to Antigua and Barbuda. He believes it could prove to be a real test for the prime minister.

“This is a test of Canada’s diversification for trade and its middle power strategy,” said Appleton.

“And this is one that Canada can pass. Traditionally, we were exceptionally strong with the Commonwealth.”

Appleton points to Canada shifting trade position over the years, moving closer to the U.S. He believes now could be an opportunity for Canada to move back towards the Commonwealth.

“In some ways - it is a test of the new Carney foreign policy - working with other states with the U.S. not present,” he said.

“For Canada, the real opportunity at CHOGM is to move deals already on the table, with India, Southeast Asia and the U.K. and to modernize a one-way Caribbean preference program that the region has found hard to use.”

items.title: Christopher Liew: Warning signs your parents’ finances are off track
items.description: Personal finance contributor Christopher Liew goes over the warning signs that your parents are struggling financially, and how to step in without wrecking your own retirement.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[(Marcus Aurelius / Pexels.com)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: Personal finance contributor Christopher Liew goes over the warning signs that your parents are struggling financially, and how to step in without wrecking your own retirement.
items.body:
Christopher Liew is a CFP® professional and CFA charterholder. He shares insights on personal finance with thousands of Canadian readers at Blueprint Financial.

A lot of us grow up assuming our parents have money figured out. They paid the bills, worried about our tuition, and never asked us for a thing. So when that starts to change, it can sneak up on you.

In my experience, by the time a parent asks for help, the problem has been building for years. Below, I’ll walk through the warning signs that you may be about to become your parents’ financial safety net, and how to step in without wrecking your own retirement.

Why more families are feeling this now

The pressure on retirees is growing. In the National Institute on Ageing’s 2025 survey, only 29 per cent of Canadians 50 and older who haven’t retired yet said they could afford to retire when they wanted, down from 35 per cent in 2022.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

The people stepping in are stretched too. As CTV News reported in May, more than half of Canada’s caregivers are juggling paid work alongside caring for a loved one, and many say the pressure is becoming too much.

That being said, money trouble doesn’t always look like a crisis. From what I’ve seen with clients, it shows up in small ways first.

1. They’re paying everyday bills with credit or the house

If your parents are carrying a credit card balance month to month, opening a line of credit, or tapping a home equity line of credit (HELOC) to cover groceries and property tax, pay attention. Borrowing for a new roof is one thing. Borrowing to keep the lights on means their income no longer covers their life.

Home equity is the one that worries me most. A reverse mortgage or HELOC can make sense as part of a real plan, but when it’s used to plug a monthly gap, the interest quietly eats the cushion they’ll need for care later.

You may never see their statements, but you’ll notice the clues: talk of consolidating debt, new cards showing up in the mail, or a sudden interest in refinancing a house they owned outright. If you’re seeing more than one of these, it’s worth a gentle question the next time you visit.

2. Their income is mostly CPP and OAS

In my view, CPP and OAS were never meant to fund a whole retirement on their own. If your parents don’t have a workplace pension or meaningful RRSP or RRIF savings, they may be living right at the edge.

One way to gauge it is the Guaranteed Income Supplement, which tops up low-income seniors. A single senior needs annual income (not counting OAS) under $23,112 to qualify, so a parent anywhere near that line has very little room for surprises. GIS is based on the previous year’s tax return, so make sure they’re still filing every spring.

I’d also watch for a parent who started CPP at 60 because they needed the cash, not as a strategy. Taking it early cuts the payment by up to 36 per cent, and that reduction is permanent.

3. They’ve started asking for help “just this once”

The first request might be small. A car repair, a dental bill, a month of rent. Saying yes is natural, and I’d never tell you not to help your parents, but one-off help has a way of turning into a monthly transfer.

Before you commit to anything regular, figure out what you can give without pausing your own RRSP or TFSA contributions. One of the biggest regrets I see in retirees is giving money to family before securing their own future, and I walked through that and nine other regrets in a recent Blueprint Financial video. The same logic applies when the money flows up to your parents instead of down to your kids.

And if you have kids, you could be squeezed from both directions. In a 2026 BMO survey, 49 per cent of Canadians said they plan to help their adult children financially, and 83 per cent of that group said they understand it will hurt their own retirement.

4. There’s no clear plan if their health changes

This is the sign that turns a manageable situation into an emergency. If you don’t know where their accounts are, whether they have a will, or who holds power of attorney, you’ll be scrambling at the worst possible time.

You don’t need every detail on Day 1. I’d start with a simple list of where their accounts are, copies of their will and power of attorney documents, and the name of anyone who already helps them with money, like an accountant or advisor.

I covered how to start that conversation in my CTV News column on talking to aging parents about money. If you’re also noticing confusion around bills or unusual withdrawals, I wrote about those red flags in my piece on money mistakes that can signal cognitive decline.

If your parent relies on you for basics like food and shelter because of a physical or mental infirmity, look into the federal Canada caregiver credit. They don’t have to live with you to qualify.

Final thoughts

Spotting these signs doesn’t mean your parents failed, and it doesn’t mean you’re on the hook forever. It means you still have time, which is the most valuable thing you can have here.

Have the honest conversation early, decide what you can realistically offer, and protect your own plan while you do it. Helping your parents shouldn’t turn you into the next generation that can’t afford to retire.

items._ogDesc: According to a website launched by the National Taxpayers Union Foundation (NTUF), tariffs cost Michigan households more than in any other state.
items.body:
OTTAWA – No where in the U.S. will tariffs be more top of mind for midterm voters than in Michigan. According to a website launched by the National Taxpayers Union Foundation (NTUF), tariffs cost Michigan households more than in any other state. U.S. President Donald Trump’s taxes cost per household in the Wolverine state is more than US$5,600.

Twenty-five per cent auto tariffs imposed by Trump in 2025, have contributed to that cost in the state, which is the heart of the American automotive industry. The highly integrated supply chain with Canada is making it even more painful for people who live and work in Michigan. If there is no trade deal with Canada by January 2027, auto tariffs on Canadian-made cars, trucks and auto parts will double to 50 per cent.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

“It’s two countries, one region,” said Sandy Baruah, president and CEO of the Detroit Regional Chamber speaking about the bilateral relationship between Canada and the U.S. “We also want our companies in the United States that actually build the facilities, that rehab and retool the facilities… to be able to do business in both the United States and Canada, equally well.”

Baruah told CTV News that ever since section 232 tariffs were imposed on Canadian steel, aluminum and autos, most businesses are waiting to make any kind of significant investment on either side of the border.

“Right now, they’re (companies) still a little frozen because they don’t know what the long-term trajectory is,” said Baruah. “If you’re a CEO of a publicly traded company, you’re saying, ‘well, let’s just see what we can do over the next couple of years, and let’s see where we go.’”

According to the National Taxpayers Union Foundation, Michigan is the third most affected by tariffs of all American states. The recent NTUF report shows importers that bring goods into Michigan have paid more than $23 billion in tariffs in the last 22 months.

The unpopularity of those taxes has bled into the hotly contested Senate race with the Republican candidate Mike Rogers even calling for an end to the trade war with Canada. In October the former congressman released a video ad pitching a truce with the U.S.’ northern neighbour.

“Here in Michigan, we know that Canada is not our enemy. We need to end this tariff war now,” said Rogers in the video, adding that if he’s elected the state’s senator he will “bring both parties together to lower your prices.”

It’s one of the rare times both Republican and Democratic candidates are on the same side of an issue with candidate Abdul El-Sayed calling Trump’s tariffs on Canadian goods “dumb” in a TV ad.

Despite the consensus on tariffs, El-Sayed is consistently polling ahead of Rogers leading up to Tuesday’s vote. With affordability being one of the central campaign issues of the midterms, the Republican record is causing issues for candidates running under the GOP banner, according to CTV News’ U.S. political analyst Eric Ham.

“That is clearly one of the drivers that we’re seeing why Republicans are having such a difficult time, because there (Michigan), it’s all about the economy,” said Ham.

According to Ham, the problem is further compounded by the so-called “Reagan Democrats.” That type of voter is traditionally registered as a democratic voter who is most commonly a blue-collar worker in the rust belt, like Michigan. They’ve earned the moniker because they’re democrats who would vote for former republican president Ronald Reagan. However, Ham isn’t sure that will happen during Tuesday’s midterms.

“What we’re seeing now in this election, even those Reagan Democrats are becoming increasingly problematic for people like Mike Rogers,” said Ham.

A number of polls show Trump’s approval rating in the state of Michigan at a record low in the 30 per cent range. A major drop from the 2024 presidential election, where Trump won the state with 49.7 per cent of the vote to Kamala Harris’ 48.3 per cent. It was a narrow victory, but enough for Trump to flip Michigan back into the Republican win column.

Keeping the state red could be a tall task, considering the current affordability crisis in Michigan and across the United States. According to the Pew Research Centre survey conducted in August, 60 per cent of Americans say that don’t currently have enough income to lead the kind of life they want.

In that same survey, nearly one-in-three respondents said, “they worry every day or nearly every day about the cost of health care and the amount of debt they have.” Twenty-seven per cent of people said they cannot pay some of their monthly bills or can only make partial payments, while more than half say they have not been able to save money for the future.

items.title: U.S. government has new rules on flight delays. Will it affect Canadian travellers?
items.description: New U.S. government rules on flight disruptions coming into force early next year could affect passengers coming from Canada, though experts are divided on whether they will have a significant impact.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Travellers stand in line as some flights are delayed at Houston Hobby Airport on March 16, 2026. (Ashley Landis / AP Photo)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Ashley Landis</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: New U.S. government rules on flight disruptions coming into force early next year could affect passengers coming from Canada, though experts are divided on whether they will have a significant impact.
items.body:
New U.S. government rules on flight disruptions coming into force early next year could affect passengers coming from Canada, though experts are divided on whether they will have a significant impact.

The U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT), which published the new rules on the Federal Register daily journal in September, is reclassifying 10 types of events that cause flight delays and cancellations as outside the airline’s control. These events include a passenger’s death, unscheduled mechanical issues, severe weather, cybersecurity attacks and potential tech outages.

The rule was supposed to take effect Oct. 19 but was postponed until Feb. 1, 2027.

The department acknowledged in the notice that “the total value of amenities and compensation currently provided by air carriers to consumers will be reduced under this final rule.”

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

Katy Nastro, a travel industry expert based in New York, said the new rules may mean travellers won’t be entitled to the same type of protections they used to have.

“So basically, it’s taking some of what was the responsibility of the airlines and recategorizing them … outside of the airline’s control,” Katy Nastro, a travel industry expert based in New York, said in a video interview with CTVNews.ca on Friday. “And very simply, for travellers, that means you may not be entitled to the same type of protections that you are now.”

“Now, when this new rule goes into effect, you as a passenger, if you are impacted due to an unscheduled maintenance event, this is outside of the airline’s control, meaning that they’re not now forced, or really obliged, to provide a hotel voucher or a meal voucher,” she added.

Airline passenger advocacy group FlyersRights is suing the U.S. Department of Transportation over the rules, which they say shift the costs from airline delays to passengers.

“A change in reporting classifications is not permission to reduce passenger rights,” Paul Hudson, president of FlyersRights, said in a news release Friday. “... The rule sneakily transfers costs from airlines back to passengers for delays involving mechanical problems that are the responsibility and fault of the airlines.”

Nastro, a correspondent with the Flighty flight-tracker app, said the change will affect anyone “travelling within the U.S., to the U.S., or from the U.S.,” regardless of their nationality or the airline, if their flight experiences certain types of disruptions that are now outside the airline’s control.

“In certain circumstances, it does grey the disruption category for consumers,” Nastro said. “This new regulation … just makes it even more confusing for travellers when they’re trying to navigate what exactly they’re entitled to in terms of disruption protections.”

Under the current DOT regulations, Nastro said disrupted flights may allow travellers to get hotel or meal vouchers, rebook flights or get refunds.

Gábor Lukács, president of Air Passenger Rights, said he believes the new rules may have a “minimal” impact on Canadian travellers flying to or from the U.S. because they would have some rights under the Canadian Air Passenger Protection Regulations.

However, he said Canada’s passenger protection regulations are “weak” with rules that are “unnecessarily complex” and “very difficult to enforce.”

He said the U.S. rule change’s effect is “primarily administrative,” because it involves how flight disruptions are being reported and passengers aren’t compensated in cash for flight disruptions in the U.S.

Lukács said the main issue with the new rules will be unexpected maintenance issues, which he said is “completely unreasonable.”

items._ogDesc: As Ottawa and the EU explore ways of working closer together, negotiations are now underway to make Canada a full participant in the Erasmus+ program.
items.body:
OTTAWA – For first year student Riley Alliman, the possibility of studying in Europe one day is an exciting proposition.

“I think I would gain better connections in the world and advance my career,” she said.

Alliman is a student of biopharmaceutical science at the University of Ottawa, and she said her hope is to become a medical researcher.

Adding that the opportunity to conduct some of her studies in a European Union country would allow her to broaden her expertise and learn how scientists elsewhere approach the same challenges.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

“It allows us to further our knowledge in how other places are doing things, versus how maybe here we have different ideas of how we might do research in things like Parkinson’s, because that’s what I’m really into,” she said.

It’s that kind of enthusiasm that officials hope will fuel interest in the EU’s student scholarship program known as Erasmus+, in which Canada already participates. But as Ottawa and the EU explore ways of working closer together, negotiations are now underway to make Canada a full participant in the program.

If that happened, it would mean Canadian students would have access to grants and scholarships that would allow them to study in an EU country. It could also facilitate more transatlantic co-operation and research partnerships. That in turn could lead to economic growth, which is one reason why Canada and the EU are coming together in the first place.

“Ultimately, students gain from those experiences, and that certainly will influence perhaps their own trajectories in the future,” said Larissa Bezo, president and CEO of the Canadian Bureau for International Studies. “But we’re also talking about strengthening Canada’s talent pipeline while building lasting connections with Europe that support research, innovation, and ultimately economic growth.”

Jeremy Kinsman, a former Canadian ambassador to the EU, says the exchange is also a useful tool for bringing citizens of Canada and the European bloc closer together.

“It was always at the foundation of the European political project that if you get people to work together,” he said, “Then you’ll forge a sense of functional achievement much more easily. You’re not strangers anymore. You’re partners.”

Partners that work together in research, technology and industry, but also share values that are increasingly challenged around the world.

“I think when they’re talking about values, people think of democracy and civil rule by law,” said Kinsman. “But it’s much more than that. It’s internationalist values of co-operation, which Canada has been committed to since the end of the Second World War. The building of an international system that’s institutional, that enables countries to come together to do what they have to do.”

“No one country can do that alone, and they do much better in concert,” he added.

Still, there are questions about cost, and how much Canada would have to pay to participate in the Erasmus+ program.

Talks are now underway, as Canadian and EU officials also explore a potential “associate EU membership” for Canada.

items._ogDesc: Prime Minister Mark Carney said he had a good conversation with U.S. President Donald Trump on trade relations
items.body:
Prime Minister Mark Carney said he had a “good conversation” with U.S. President Donald Trump on trade relations.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

In an X post on Sunday, Carney said the talk builds on “recent constructive discussions” on a prospective Canada-U.S. trade deal.

The Prime Minister’s Office told CTV News the call happened on Saturday.”

Carney described the deal as one that would “create jobs for our workers, boost affordability for families, and fully respect Canada’s languages, culture, and sovereignty.”

He added that Canadian and U.S. representatives will be working in the coming weeks to “deliver that outcome.”

Trump told reporters Sunday afternoon that they had a “concept of a very good deal with Canada.”

“We’ve been losing money for many years with Canada... many many years, 70-75 years. So, we are now very close to having a deal,” he said.

“I spoke with the prime minister the other day. I spoke to him again yesterday, and we have the concept of a deal that’s going to be great for our farmers, great for our country, and it’ll be fine for Canada too.”

A statement from the White House said the Trump administration “welcomes continued engagement with Canada” as they work towards finalizing details of a deal that will “deliver meaningful results for the American people.”

Meanwhile, the minister in charge of Canada-U.S. trade, Dominic LeBlanc’s office told CTV News Sunday that he is not in Washington at the moment, and has nothing more to share about whether he plans to travel in the coming days.

‘Deliver real results’

At a press conference the same day, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre encouraged Carney to “get a great deal.” He said everyday Canadians can’t afford to wait for a trade deal with the U.S.

“The prime minister promised in the last election he would get an even better deal than we had before. He’s broken that promise so far,” he said. “It’s time for Mr. Carney to put the big talk in the past and deliver real results.”

The prime minister told reporters on Monday that the Trump administration has been “coming closer” to Canada’s position on the trade talks, following CTV News reporting that the White House has become more amenable due to vulnerabilities ahead of the midterm elections.

Last week, multiple sources told CTV News that the Americans seem to show more interest in inking a deal than they have “in all the weeks prior.”

Carney on Monday, added that he can’t guarantee Trump will respect anything they sign.

“I don’t know that,” he said, when specifically asked how he knows the U.S. president will sign in pen.

He reiterated interest in an agreement that benefits “all Canadians, with very clear bottom lines, red lines.”

“Which means that we were not willing to sign what was offered in August,” he said.

U.S. midterms exert pressure

Tuesday’s midterm election brings high stakes for both parties. A Democrat wave could see a Congressional check to Trump’s unprecedented use of executive powers during the remainder of his tenure.

Polling shows Democrats are favoured to take the House, where a net gain of three seats would give them a majority. The future of the Senate is less clear, where some polling shows a Democrat net gain of four seats is within reach.

While Trump’s first term rattled the bilateral relationship between Canada and the U.S., his second term blew it up. Canada was an early target of Trump’s tariffs and Canadians were shocked and appalled by the president’s repeated threats of annexation.

Tensions escalated further in August when trade talks collapsed. Trump slapped an array of Canadian goods with 50 per cent tariffs, banned imports of other Canadian products and signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America.

The trade war is deeply unpopular in states like Michigan and Maine, where tight Senate races ultimately could decide which party gains congressional control.

But even if Democrats emerge triumphant next week, or win the White House in 2028, it’s not clear that Trump’s tariff wall would suddenly drop.

Carney said last week that Canada was not yet in a position to reach a trade deal with Trump’s administration.

On his way into the weekly Liberal national caucus meeting on Parliament Hill, Carney said on Wednesday that Ottawa was prepared to make a deal only when it suits Canadians’ interests.

items._ogDesc: Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is pushing for the federal government to eliminate all federal taxes on diesel until Canada Day, part of a list of demands ahead of the budget being tabled on Nov. 5.
items.body:
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is pushing for the federal government to eliminate all federal taxes on diesel until Canada Day, part of a list of demands ahead of the budget being tabled on Thursday.

In a letter to Prime Minister Mark Carney, Poilievre said suspending the GST on fuel until summer and permanently scrapping the fuel standard tax would save Canadians money, whether they’re buying groceries or toys for Christmas.

In the letter, Poilievre also calls for the Liberal government to cut what he called wasteful and inflationary spending, adding that the government should cut bureaucracy. The federal government has pledged to slash the public service by 10 per cent by the end of the 2028-29 fiscal year — eliminating about 40,000 jobs.

Poilievre also said the Carney government should fulfil promises to reduce both the debt-to-GDP ratio and deficit-to-GDP. He said keeping his word to reduce the debt and deficit as a share of the economy is the bare minimum Carney can do.

Poilievre held a news conference alongside the Canadian Taxpayers Federation on Sunday. He stood in front of a truck displaying a federal “debt clock” as he gave remarks.

“Carney promised affordability, yet everything costs more since he got here,” Poilievre said. “Carney is out of touch, his costs are out of control and Canadians are out of money.”

Midway through the press conference, the “debt clock” display turned off and staff scrambled to fix it.

The Parliamentary Budget Office has predicted that the government will not meet its fiscal anchor of maintaining a declining deficit-to-GDP ratio; instead, the office expects the measure to rise in 2027-28 and 2029-30.

The office also expects a $63.3-billion deficit in fiscal 2026-27, down from a forecast of $71.8 billion in its June outlook. It sees annual deficit levels peaking at $70.2 billion the following year.

Poilievre said Carney’s government has the biggest deficit ever outside of the COVID-19 pandemic and the highest spending as a share of GDP since the 1990s debt crisis.

He said the prime minister has helped drive up the cost of basic living expenses that people can’t afford.

“You promised affordability. Yet everything is more expensive since you took office. While you cannot control things outside Canada, your decisions at home have only made things worse,” the letter said.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne has said the budget will “outline the next steps in our plan to build a stronger, more resilient and more affordable Canada.”

The upcoming fiscal plan will be the second delivered under Carney and comes as Canada’s economy faces sharp headwinds from U.S. tariffs and other geopolitical forces.

Since taking office, Carney has tried to reorient federal spending away from the day-to-day operations of government and instead focus borrowing on an aggressive infrastructure agenda.

Canada’s economy showed some resilience in the second quarter but growth is under fresh pressure after the collapse of trade talks with the United States in August.

“The budget should save Canadians money and jobs and put Canada first,” Poilievre said Sunday.

items._ogDesc: United States defence and aerospace giant Lockheed Martin has acquired Nova Scotia-based undersea defence company Ultra Maritime for $3.45 billion.
items.body:
DARTMOUTH — United States defence and aerospace giant Lockheed Martin has acquired Nova Scotia-based undersea defence company Ultra Maritime for $3.45 billion.

Lockheed Martin completed its acquisition of Ultra Maritime last week after the two companies signed a deal in July.

Lockheed Martin says it had been an investor in Ultra Maritime since 2022.

Based in Dartmouth, N.S., and founded in 1947 as Cossar (Canada) Ltd., Ultra Maritime specializes in advanced undersea and anti-submarine warfare.

The company’s website says it manufactures sonar solutions, sonobuoys and torpedo defence systems to detect and track submarine threats for allied navies in more than 30 countries, including Canada and the U.S.

Ultra Maritime says it employs about 2,000 people in five countries, and as of last year, the federal government said the company employed more than 250 people in Dartmouth, N.S.

Lockheed Martin’s president of Rotary and Mission Systems, Stephanie Hill, says the acquisition of Ultra Maritime will allow it to meet the growing demand for undersea warfare capability worldwide.

“By joining forces with Ultra Maritime, we’re accelerating our commitment to deliver the most advanced undersea and anti-submarine warfare capabilities to our U.S. and allied partners across the globe,” said a statement from Hill.

The announcement comes after a recent surge in investment in defence and shipbuilding in Nova Scotia.

After inking the deal with Ultra Maritime, Lockheed Martin Canada also partnered with Invest Nova Scotia in July, committing to adding up to 320 skilled jobs in the province within the next five years.

It says it will add up to $126 million in salaries and benefits to the local economy based on growing demand for its Canadian-made combat management system.

Earlier that month, Prime Minister Mark Carney also announced that German firm TKMS was the preferred bidder to build 12 new submarines for the Royal Canadian Navy.

The deal is expected to increase the number of sailors, maintenance workers and naval suppliers in Halifax, home to Canada’s largest naval base.

items._ogDesc: This week’s top stories include Canada’s real estate spreading beyond Ontario and BC, and the CMHC warns mortgage arrears are set to rise.
items.body:
Time for your cheat sheet on this week’s top stories.

Canadian Real Estate

Canadian GDP Stalls, Propped Up By Retail And Credit Cards

Canadian economic output is starting to struggle. Real GDP was flat for a second straight month in August, with only 9 out of 20 industrial sectors showing growth. Stalling appears to be an optimistic take though, as the details are a little more ominous. The pillars supporting the data were higher retail sales (mostly food) and credit card use. In other words, grocery spending and credit card debt are keeping the economy afloat. That’s more concerning given the increasing use of credit cards to make ends meet, according to TransUnion.

Canada’s Housing Agency Forecasts Surge In Mortgage Arrears, But It May Be Worse

The arrears rate at Canadian banks has made an aggressive climb and it’s not over, warns the CMHC. The CBA arrears rate has more than doubled from record lows over the past 5 years, hitting 0.29% in July—an 11-year high. The rate will climb through mid-2027, the end of the agency’s forecast period. They cite price corrections in BC and Ontario persisting as the key reason. However, prices are near record highs in other provinces and have only just begun to correct, suggesting risk is further to the upside.

Bank of Canada Sees Elevated Inflation Into 2028, Housing To Remain Weak

The Bank of Canada’s (BoC) got 99 problems and inflation’s just one—until 2028, at least that’s what they think. This week the BoC hiked its overnight rate to 2.5%, its first hike in over 3 years. Higher energy prices will trickle into broader consumer inflation, warns the BoC. As a result, headline CPI’s annual growth will remain above 3% into late 2027, returning to the 2% target by mid-2028. Just 2 more years to flatten the (inflation) curve?

Canadian Real Estate Correction Now Spreading To Other Provinces

Prices across the country surged when rates were cut in 2020. The national index has fallen 22.5% since prices peaked in 2022, when rates began to normalize. However, that correction was almost entirely the work of Ontario and—to a lesser extent—BC. The rest of the provinces remain near record highs, but that may be finally changing. Prices in some of those provinces have recently begun to make record-setting declines.

Bank of Canada Study Warns Rate Cuts Mostly Create Demand, Not Supply

BoC researchers looked at the impact of monetary stimulus on housing supply. They found that rate cuts during a housing boom boost home building by 6%, but only 20% of that is due to financing. The remaining 80% of stimulus comes from the excess demand, as profits and prices rise too. They warn ignoring shelter costs during a housing boom can lead to an aggressive climb in prices. However, there’s an area of shelter inflation the BoC should ignore—mortgage interest. Mortgage interest’s inclusion in CPI creates a self-reinforcing feedback loop. Cutting rates reduces mortgage interest, signaling the need for more rate cuts. It’s a problem we’ve noted before, warning the circular logic is avoided by most countries.

Ontario Real Estate

Ontario Mortgage Arrears To Keep Surging, Led by Toronto: CMHC

Ontario’s mortgage arrears rate at banks hit 0.32% in Q2 2026, 52% higher than last year and 5x the low in 2022. That’s only the bank rate though, which makes the picture look better than reality. High-risk borrowers get booted to mortgage investment entities (MIEs), where risk is exploding. MIEs have seen the arrears rate around Greater Toronto surge from 3% in Q3 2023 to 11.1% in Q1 2026, 3x the national MIE rate. They may only be a small share of national activity, but the bulk of their business is concentrated in one area—along with risk.

items.description: The CMAs are Canada's top mortgage industry night — and the ROI extends well beyond individual recognition
items.content: <p>The CMAs are Canada's top mortgage industry night — and the ROI extends well beyond individual recognition</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0270_637746489857378440.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: The CMAs are Canada's top mortgage industry night — and the ROI extends well beyond individual recognition
items.body:
For mortgage brokers and brokerage leaders across Canada, the Canadian Mortgage Awards (CMAs) have long represented the industry's highest standard of professional recognition.

Now in their 20th year, the CMAs are set to take place on November 25 at Rebel Toronto — and this milestone edition makes a compelling case for attending not as an individual, but as a team.

While individual nominations drive the night's agenda, the strategic value of group attendance at the CMAs extends far beyond the trophy.

For brokerages thinking seriously about recruitment, retention, culture, and competitive positioning, booking a table, or a block of seats, is increasingly less a luxury and more a sound business decision.

The case for a team night out

Mortgage brokerage is, at its core, a people business. The culture a firm builds internally — how it celebrates wins, how it acknowledges hard work, how it signals that individual effort is seen — has a direct effect on retention.

In an industry where top brokers face constant competition for their services, that culture gap can be costly.

Attending the CMAs as a group is one of the more tangible ways a brokerage can make that message concrete.

The event's November 25 evening at Rebel Toronto begins with a cocktail reception from 6:00 p.m. to 7:30 p.m., followed by the awards ceremony and dinner banquet until 10:30 p.m., with a post-awards celebration running well into the night.

It is not a brief industry function — it is a full evening designed, in the words of the organizers, for sharing insights, networking and building connections.

For a brokerage principal, bringing a group of agents or support staff signals something that a memo cannot: that their contributions are worth celebrating in public, before their peers, in the same room as hundreds of the foremost mortgage professionals and key executives from top Canadian organizations.

Secure a table at the 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards and celebrate your team’s achievements alongside industry leaders, innovators, and top-performing professionals from across the country. #MortgageAwardsCA Book your table today: https://t.co/SSKx4yuft5 https://t.co/f31Lgyrrzt — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 28, 2026

Recognition that reaches beyond the individual

The CMAs span 26 award categories, recognising brokers, brokerages, lenders, business development managers, underwriters, and service providers across the Canadian mortgage industry.

Across those categories, the awards are designed to reflect not just individual performance but the collective effort behind it.

When a broker wins, or is named an excellence awardee ahead of the November gala, the recognition lands in Canadian Mortgage Professional (CMP) magazine and across its online channels.

The profiles and features generated from shortlistings and wins carry the names of those firms into editorial content that reaches CMP's readership throughout the year. For a brokerage, that coverage is institutional: it attaches to the firm's brand, not only to the individual.

That makes the case for corporate attendance straightforward. A team present in the room when a colleague is recognised associates the brokerage with the win in a way that a congratulatory email the next morning cannot replicate.

The CMAs have been described by past winners, including Steven Ranson of HomeEquity Bank in Toronto, as "iconic" — an event where the industry turns out to take stock of itself. Being part of that moment, collectively, carries a different weight than watching it from outside.

For brokerages that have not yet submitted a nomination, the deadline has passed for the 2026 cycle, with excellence awardees already announced in September.

But the event itself remains open to the industry, and registering as a group for the CMAs gala at Rebel Toronto is a separate matter from the nomination process.

The networking case for corporate attendance

Beyond recognition, the CMAs function as one of the most concentrated networking events on the Canadian mortgage calendar.

Hundreds of senior professionals — brokers, lenders, aggregators, and executives — gather in a single venue for an evening built around industry conversation.

The cocktail reception that opens the night is specifically designed to facilitate that kind of contact before the formal programme begins.

For a junior broker or an agent new to the industry, attending the CMAs alongside experienced colleagues offers a different kind of access.

The introductions that happen organically in rooms like Rebel Toronto — between a new agent and a business development manager from a major lender, or between a brokerage's team and a potential referral partner — are not easily manufactured in any other setting.

A group presence makes those introductions more natural: arriving as a team, rather than alone, lowers the social friction of a large industry event.

For mortgage professionals seeking deeper insight into how Canada's top brokerages and lenders benchmark their performance, events like the CMAs serve as a live read on where the industry's weight is shifting — which firms are growing, which categories are most competitive, and which names are emerging.

That intelligence, absorbed in a room with peers, is harder to replicate through trade coverage alone.

The CMA organizers note that the event "provides the ideal setting for an evening tailor-made for sharing insights, networking and building connections."

A brokerage that treats the evening as a strategic exercise, briefing its staff on who else will be in the room and what conversations are worth having, is likely to leave with more than a photograph.

Registration is open at canadianmortgageawards.com.

items._ogDesc: MCAN Financial Group grows managed assets to $9.4 billion as insured originations surge 27%
items.body:
MCAN Mortgage Corporation d/b/a MCAN Financial Group, Canada’s federally regulated mortgage investment corporation (MIC), reported a 21% rise in total assets under management to $9.4 billion for the nine months ended September 30.

Strong residential mortgage originations, expanding securitization activity, and steady broker-driven renewals each contributed to the result.

Net interest income for Q3 2026 rose 12% to $26.7 million compared with Q3 2025.

Year-to-date net income climbed 16% to $66.2 million, underpinned by higher lending volumes and income from MCAP Commercial LP, the company’s strategic partner.

Quarterly net income declined 6% to $19.2 million on unrealized losses in MCAN’s securities portfolio.

Broker-driven volumes lift residential mortgage assets

Residential mortgage assets reached $5.1 billion at September 30, up 11% year to date. Insured assets grew 13% to $3.7 billion; uninsured assets rose 8% to $1.4 billion.

Against the same nine months of 2025, insured originations surged 27% and uninsured originations rose 13%, building on MCAN’s expanding origination base through the first half of 2026, when second-quarter net income jumped 19%.

“Strong growth in our assets under management reflects the continued execution of our strategy,” said Derek Sutherland, chief executive officer of MCAN Financial Group.

“Our business continues to perform well in all our main product lines, despite uncertainty in the broader economic environment, supported by strong mortgage originations and renewals, disciplined pricing and hedging strategies, as well as our strategic partnership with MCAP. We believe we are well-reserved in our allowance for credit losses and our sound underwriting practices ensure our credit quality remains resilient.”

That resilience is built on the broker channel. Speaking in a recent Canadian Mortgage Professional roundtable examining Canada’s evolving alternative lending landscape for mortgage brokers, Avish Buck, senior vice-president and chief operating officer of MCAN Financial Group and president of MCAN Home Mortgage Corp in Toronto, said: “When a broker works with MCAN, it means they trust us with their client, and that’s something we take seriously. Trust is the core of any relationship.”

Construction mortgages rise 9%, but impairments climb

Construction and commercial mortgage balances grew 9% year to date to $1.3 billion, with loan advances of $359 million through September 30.

Project extensions tied to permitting and zoning delays, as well as a more cautious economic environment, have affected parts of the portfolio.

The impaired non-securitized mortgage ratio rose to 2.31% from 1.69% at December 31, 2025, driven by construction loans and uninsured residential mortgages under asset recovery.

Provisions for credit losses totalled $5.7 million year to date. Average loan-to-value ratios of 68.2% on uninsured residential mortgages and 62.8% on construction loans point to credit quality challenges facing Canadian mortgage lenders that remain manageable for a conservatively underwritten book.

In October, MCAN launched an additional uninsured residential mortgage securitization program with a major Canadian bank to further diversify funding.

Year-to-date income from MCAP reached $27.6 million, up 8%. The board declared a fourth-quarter dividend of $0.43 per share, payable January 4, 2027 to shareholders of record December 15.

items.description: Three Bay Street analysts warn Q3 growth is tracking well short of the Bank of Canada’s forecast
items.content: <p>Three Bay Street analysts warn Q3 growth is tracking well short of the Bank of Canada’s forecast</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639289794928292353.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Three Bay Street analysts warn Q3 growth is tracking well short of the Bank of Canada’s forecast
items.body:
Canada’s economy delivered little in August, with real gross domestic product (GDP) essentially flat for a second consecutive month — trailing both market expectations and Statistics Canada’s preliminary estimate of 0.2% growth, raising fresh questions about the Bank of Canada’s decision to raise interest rates last week.

The August result follows a broadly flat July, marking a deceleration from the 3.3% annualized growth recorded in Canada’s second quarter of 2026.

With Statistics Canada’s advance estimate projecting a further 0.1% decline in September, Q3 GDP is now tracking at approximately 1.3% annualized, well below the Bank of Canada’s 2.0% projection in its October 2026 Monetary Policy Report (MPR).

The composition of August was mixed. Retail activity rose sharply, suggesting resilient household spending despite higher borrowing and energy costs.

Manufacturing output and engineering construction also gained, while wholesale trade, public administration, and oil and gas extraction all declined.

Statistics Canada reported no growth in August GDP and an estimated decline in September, suggesting third-quarter growth may fall short of the Bank of Canada’s expectations following its latest interest rate increase. https://t.co/CCruoYeDlc — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 30, 2026

Mixed signals for the central bank

On October 28, the Bank of Canada raised its overnight rate by 25 basis points to 2.50%, its first hike since July 2023. Economists characterized the move as risk management, though softer GDP data complicates that framing.

Marc Ercolao, economist at TD Economics in Toronto, wrote that August’s result “may cast a little more doubt around the durability of the recovery heading into 2027,” noting that softer fourth-quarter momentum “raises the bar” for the Bank’s 2027 growth forecast, “particularly with trade uncertainty and higher energy costs still clouding the outlook.”

Andrew Grantham, senior economist at CIBC Economics in Toronto, offered a blunter take. August data, he wrote, showed that “all of the growth in Q3 came from the strong handoff at the end of the second quarter, and that throughout the period the economy actually stagnated.”

Greater slack, he added, should limit firms’ ability to pass through higher energy costs to consumers — capping core inflation below the Bank of Canada’s own MPR projections.

Abbey Xu, economist at RBC in Toronto, described the August composition as “somewhat better than the headline,” noting that retail resilience and engineering construction gains were consistent with an economy still expanding, “albeit unevenly and at a more moderate pace.”

What the data means for brokers

For mortgage professionals navigating Canada’s mounting 2026 mortgage renewal pressures, the Q3 shortfall arrives at a difficult moment.

Jessica Rickerby, president of the Canadian Mortgage Brokers Association of Ontario (CMBA Ontario) in Toronto, told Canadian Mortgage Professional: “While inflation is a key concern of Ontarians, so is housing affordability. The difference is that affordability is a pressing issue right now, whereas inflation is – at present – a hypothetical.”

With the next Bank of Canada rate decision on December 9, the small-business outlook for Canada’s mortgage market already signals a rougher fourth quarter, and October and November GDP prints will carry unusual weight.

The Canadian economy has stalled, and the details offer little reassurance. Real GDP was flat in August for a second straight month, according to Statistics Canada (StatCan). Retail and credit card activity helped support output, an ominous combination as credit industry reports point to rising balances and delinquencies. The agency’s preliminary September estimate suggests that stagnation would be good news compared to what lies ahead.

Canada’s Economy Stalls For A Second Consecutive Month

Canadian economic output stalled for another month. Following a flat July, real GDP remained “essentially unchanged” in August. Just 9 of 20 industrial sectors expanded, with goods-producing industries rising 0.1% but tamed by a 0.1% drop in services. The stagnation follows massive jumps in April (+0.6%), May (+0.3%), and June (+0.4%), highlighting an abrupt and rapid loss of momentum.

Retail and Credit Card Activity Helping To Prop Up the Economy

The latest GDP report shows the economy may be living on borrowed time. One of the key areas of growth is retail output, rising 1.2% in August, led by vehicle dealers and food retailers. Also providing a boost was finance and insurance, which advanced 0.2%, with banking climbing 0.3% despite a slow mortgage market. The agency notes the growth in the latter was driven by non-mortgage lending activity, specifically credit cards.

That specific data point sounds more concerning when paired with TransUnion comments. The consumer credit reporting agency recently warned of rising balances and delinquency rates for consumers. They noted that consumers are increasingly relying on credit cards to smooth consumption. To be blunt, the read here isn’t very optimistic—consumer spending is helping to prop up the economy while borrowers increasingly rely on credit cards to make ends meet.

Canadian GDP Expected To Contract In September

Unfortunately, things are set to get worse according to the agency’s advance estimates. StatCan’s preliminary numbers point to a 0.1% drop in real GDP in September. Manufacturing and mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction are expected to lead the decline. However, the agency estimates average economic output in Q3 will still be 0.3% higher than in Q2, despite the loss of monthly momentum.

The figures also largely pre-date the latest tariff escalation. The U.S. imposed escalation only took effect in the final days of August, making September the first full month under those measures. It intensifies further as the first full month of Canada’s retaliatory tariffs won’t be seen until the October GDP data. StatCan hasn’t indicated whether its preliminary data fully captures the latest tariff escalation, leaving open the possibility of further weakness.

items.title: The BoC isn’t expecting the housing market to heat up anytime soon
items.description: Central bank sees a sluggish outlook continuing – and BMO managing director says less focus on housing wouldn’t necessarily be a bad thing
items.content: <p>Central bank sees a sluggish outlook continuing – and BMO managing director says less focus on housing wouldn’t necessarily be a bad thing</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639289754495839586.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Central bank sees a sluggish outlook continuing – and BMO managing director says less focus on housing wouldn’t necessarily be a bad thing
items.body:
The Bank of Canada doesn’t see much chance of a hotter national housing market in the near future, forecasting this week that housing will contribute essentially nothing to national economic growth in the next two years.

The central bank said in the latest Monetary Policy Report, released alongside its rate hike on Wednesday, that climbing borrowing costs will send housing-related expenses higher in 2027 and 2028, while material and equipment prices will also increase as home construction and maintenance costs rise.

That’s not to say housing and mortgage professionals will notice a sudden or sharp change, with the deep freeze that’s gripped the market over the past two years showing no sign of thawing.

Benjamin Reitzes (pictured top), managing director, Canadian rates and macro strategist at Bank of Montreal (BMO), told Canadian Mortgage Professional the central bank’s 25-basis-point increase on October 28 may have a slight negative impact on the market, but that there wasn’t much momentum to stall in the first place.

“What’s notable is that you already had mortgage rates notably higher right across the curve. So the only point where they were contained was on the variable side,” he said. “At least half the activity was coming in variable, according to the data.

“So [the hike] will provide a bit more of a dampener, I think, on the margin. Of course it makes a difference – but it’s not as if housing was booming. And so there probably is a limit to how much weaker it gets.”

Why the housing market is still slow

The main culprits for the still-sluggish housing market are well known at this stage: economic uncertainty triggered by the US-Canada trade war, and inflation concerns as a result of surging fuel costs.

That trade dispute has sparked fears of job losses and a big hit to the economy since the beginning of last year, while rising inflation was one of the main reasons the Bank of Canada raised rates on Wednesday and could hike again soon.

And while home prices have slid across many markets in 2025 and 2026, Reitzes suggested that the correction may still have a while to run.

“The reality for the housing market is that affordability is still stretched. There’s still room for prices to fall – the affordability side of things needs to improve,” he said. “I think at this point, the path of least resistance is probably still toward modestly lower prices for housing and continued softness on that front. And that’s what the Bank’s expecting.”

Affordability improved in almost every major Canadian market in September, according to ratehub.ca, but that picture could be complicated if rates continue rising in the coming months.

Population dynamics are also playing their part in the market’s slowdown. The federal government dramatically upped its immigration targets in the early years of this decade, boosting demand for housing and rental units.

Those targets have been pared back substantially, a trend that’s lowered clamour for condo rentals in major markets – most notably Toronto – and contributed to the wider housing market cooldown.

The market’s torpor has also fuelled calls among some executives for an end or revision to the foreign homebuyer ban that’s been in place since the beginning of 2023, although industry views on the matter have been mixed.

Why a less intense housing market could ultimately benefit Canada

Reitzes emphasized that a less intense focus on the housing market could be a net positive in the long run for the Canadian economy.

“Population growth is not particularly strong in Canada at the moment, and so the dynamics are challenging for housing – and that isn’t necessarily the worst thing,” he said. “Housing has… gotten too much attention over the past few decades, and it’s kind of shifting the focus toward business investment and toward driving productivity growth in Canada.

“As much as people love to focus on housing, sometimes it’s not always the best use of capital for the country. So it’s not the end of the world here that we’re going a different way.”

items.description: Grechi Carter partner and founder on the current and coming trends in private and alternative lending
items.content: <p>Grechi Carter partner and founder on the current and coming trends in private and alternative lending</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0343_639289674628824034.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Grechi Carter partner and founder on the current and coming trends in private and alternative lending
items.body:
Daniele Grechi, partner and founder at Grechi Carter Real Estate Lawyers, joins us to talk about how the private and alternative lending space has evolved, and where it’s heading. We look back at the early days of syndicate lending, loose structure and outsized returns, and how the arrival of institutional money since COVID has made private lending far more regulated and competitive.

[00:00] We're meeting a lot of people who are saying, you know, the service we used to get we're not getting anymore. The returns were just absurd for the risk levels. My general thoughts are we're close to the bottom. I think tough times make for better actions. Not every lender is doing every deal anymore.

[00:27] Fergal McAlinden: So, we are joined now by Daniele Grechi who is a partner and founder at Grechi Carter.

[00:34] Grechi Carter. Great to talk to you today. You're in an interesting space to look at how things are going in the mortgage sector and the mortgage industry as a whole. Tell us a little bit about some of the work that you're doing in the mortgage sector at the moment.

[00:46] Daniele Grechi: So, we're still quite busy with the private lending side of things. For us, the really interesting thing has been how the enforcement side of things is growing. There's obviously, with the way the market's been, a real need for that.

[01:00] I think our firm is in a very unique position because we've got a high level of expertise in that space. We've got a full team dedicated, four lawyers, three clerks. So, we can handle a high volume of work and still provide the level of service that our clients would expect.

[01:19] I know that the industry is generally kind of struggling, for lack of a better word. A lot of the big firms in this space have so much volume that we're meeting a lot of people who are saying, you know, the service we used to get we're not getting anymore. That's kind of provided a ton of opportunity for us to spread our wings and grow in this space, and we have.

[01:34] Fergal McAlinden: You mentioned you work in the private lending space. That's obviously seen a big evolution over the past few years. You mentioned that you were last year kind of pre-COVID. What have been some of the big changes that you've seen over the years in terms of how you're working with private and alternative lenders?

[01:46] Daniele Grechi: Well, it's really interesting because we've been in this space for almost 15 years now, and in the first six or seven years, it was such a different space. It was a lot of syndicate lending, a lot less structure, a lot of random different groups, small lenders, and the returns were just absurd for the risk levels that were available.

[02:05] Every year markets were going up 20%. It's sort of an easier space to operate in and because of that a ton of capital flooded to it. Since the COVID era, I think what we've seen is the flock of institutional money through the mix and they very much have professionalized the space.

[02:22] I think what we now refer to as private is kind of institutional, very regulated, very professional, extremely competitive. I think that's sort of the biggest change I've seen since we started in the business.

[02:38] Fergal McAlinden: Looking even to the next year or so, or the next few years, any kind of trends that you foresee? Do you see the space continuing to grow? Are there challenges ahead? What's in store?

[02:47] Daniele Grechi: I definitely think the space is going to grow. I think right now a lot of firms are probably going through some pain because of the change in the market, but a lot of people have adapted.

[02:58] My general thoughts are we're close to the bottom. So, hopefully things are going to move up from here. It's really forced people to have tighter processes. I think tough times make for better actions and people have had to tighten their processes, really look at their underwriting.

[03:14] And I think moving forward I see a more stable space. Opportunities are always going to be there. It's such a big market. I'm just really hoping to see the rebound in the real estate market and that everybody can get busier again.

[03:28] Fergal McAlinden: I think we're all looking ahead to that. Is there anything, Daniele, that you're speaking mostly with brokers about today or any kind of big conversations that you're hoping to have with them?

[03:36] Daniele Grechi: I mean it's always the same types of conversations. They're looking for speed, turnaround, can you handle complicated things? Is there anything different right now than we've seen in the past? No, I don't think there's anything different.

[03:48] Like I said, I think it's that theme of the people who are still working are working hard. It's tougher times, so it's forced people to become better at what they do. And that's kind of the theme right now in the real estate market.

[04:00] Fergal McAlinden: How about the event today? What's your general impressions of how it's gone?

[04:03] Daniele Grechi: A lot of energy. I've noticed a lot of people who are really, really hungry to meet as many people and learn as much as they can.

[04:12] I think it's probably tied into that, you know, not every lender is doing every deal anymore. So, you've got to go to different lenders for different needs. You've got to know your sweet spots for whatever it is that your clients need.

[04:23] So, I do really get the sense that people are here to meet different people, learn about what they do, and see how they can help them with their practice.

[04:30] Fergal McAlinden: Face-to-face conversations, it can't be overstated how important they are.

[04:34] Daniele Grechi: 100%.

[04:35] Fergal McAlinden: All right. Well, good luck with the rest of the event. Great to see you today, Daniele, and we'll talk to you soon.

[04:39] Daniele Grechi: Thanks. Great to meet you.
