items.title: Ontario Municipalities Begin Slashing Development Charges As Part Of Federal Deal
items.description:
After reaching an $8.8 billion agreement on March 30 to cut development charges, the Governments of Canada and Ontario have been busy finalizing agreements with local governments to implement the changes.

The initiative is officially known as the Development Charge Reduction Program (DCRP) and applications opened on June 1, as previously reported by STOREYS.

The program “will deliver federal and provincial funding over 10 years for housing-enabling infrastructure projects, with funding prioritized for municipalities that reduce development charges for all residential types by 30 per cent to 50 per cent or greater and maintain the reductions for at least three years.”

Municipalities levy development charges on new construction to fund infrastructure, and this program will see the federal and provincial government fund that infrastructure, allowing municipalities to lower the levies.

The first announcements were made in late-August, with Hamilton receiving $572 million and Vaughan receiving $697.2 million.

Hamilton has committed to eliminating development charges on all residential developments from March 30, 2026 to March 31, 2029, reducing the cost of building new homes by up to $100,442 per home.

The $572 million in funding — with the federal government cost-matching the provincial government — will go toward projects like the widening of Barton Street into a five-lane multi-modal road from Fruitland Road to Fifty Road, widening Rymal Road, widening Garner Road, expanding the Woodward water and wastewater treatment plant, and upgrading the capacity of the Greenhill Water Pumping Station.

A few more announcements were made in September, but the pace of announcements hit another gear this month, with agreements with 11 municipalities announced. To date, agreements announced include:

  1. Hamilton: $572 million
  2. Vaughan: $697.2 million
  3. Bradford West Gwillimbury: $94.8 million
  4. Mississauga: $404.1 million
  5. Barrie: $129.2 million
  6. St. Thomas: $19.6 million
  7. Orillia: $11.3 million
  8. Guelph: $48.3 million
  9. Sudbury: $45.3 million
  10. Essex County: $51.2 million
  11. LaSalle: $25.4 million
  12. Essex Town: $8.8 million
  13. Lakeshore: $11.8 million
  14. Kingsville: $8.4 million
  15. Windsor: $77.6 million
  16. Tecumseh: $6.8 million.

In total, the announcements amount to $2.2 billion in infrastructure funding. In most cases, the agreements will see the local government reduce development charges by 30% to 100% from March 30, 2026 to March 31, 2029.

One announcement that was slightly different was that for Mississauga, whose agreement runs from January 29, 2025 to March 31, 2029, reflecting the fact that Mississauga had previously implemented a development charge incentive program on its own, prior to the Canada-Ontario agreement.

Another announcement that was a bit more unique was that for the County of Essex, whose agreement runs from March 30, 2026 to December 31, 2030. According to the announcement, Essex County is reducing development charges on a staggered timeline. The reduction will be 100% for 2026 and 2027, 75% for 2028, 50% in 2029, and 25% in 2030.

The range of infrastructure projects the $2.2 billion in funding will go towards include road, bus, water, and wastewater infrastructure projects that are described as “housing-enabling.”

Ontario is also home to municipalities that do not levy development charges, however, and the $8.8 billion Canada-Ontario agreement recognizes that as well. In mid-August, the two governments announced a Non-Development Charge Municipalities Stream (Non-DC Stream) that will allow those governments to also receive infrastructure funding that will enable new housing development.

“Municipalities that do not levy development charges often face challenges funding infrastructure projects because they do not have access to this revenue tool,” said the two governments in the announcement. “At the same time, these municipalities face high construction costs, aging assets and significant infrastructure backlogs.”

The Development Cost Reduction Program began accepting applications under the Non-DC Stream on October 29, 2026, with additional intakes expected to be announced at a later date.

The Development Cost Reduction Program is, of course, just one half of the Canada-Ontario deal, with the other being the 13% HST rebate from April 1, 2026 to March 31, 2027. The HST relief has sparked market activity in certain areas and segments of the market, although the market has still been fairly subdued.

The HST has also been the envy of the real estate industry in British Columbia, which has continued to push for similar relief. The Governments of Canada and British Columbia reached a deal in June that was similar to the $8.8 billion Canada-Ontario deal, but it did not include the tax relief component. The deal did include development charge relief, but the program and agreements were not finalized prior to the snap election held earlier this month.

items.title: Canada’s GDP stalls, clouding Bank of Canada’s December call
items.description: Weak August data and a likely September contraction test the Bank of Canada’s resolve on rates
items.content: <p>Weak August data and a likely September contraction test the Bank of Canada’s resolve on rates</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639289647421852556.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Weak August data and a likely September contraction test the Bank of Canada’s resolve on rates
items.body:
Canada’s economy failed to grow for a second consecutive month in August, and Statistics Canada’s advance estimate for September points to a 0.1% contraction. The outcome lands below the Bank of Canada’s own projections just 48 hours after the central bank’s first rate hike since 2023.

Statistics Canada reported Friday that real gross domestic product was essentially unchanged in August. A 1.4% drop in wholesale trade and a 0.2% fall in the public sector aggregate, its first decline in six months, outweighed gains in retail trade, manufacturing, and construction.

Should the advance September estimate hold, third-quarter annualised growth would reach only 1.3%, against the Bank of Canada’s own 2% forecast.

The Bank raised its overnight rate to 2.50% on October 28, framing the move as risk management against energy-driven inflation. Friday’s GDP data offers a pointed counterpoint.

Benjamin Reitzes of BMO says the Bank of Canada's first rate hike in more than three years may not be its last, with future decisions likely hinging on economic growth, inflation trends, and incoming data over the months ahead. https://t.co/lcW0HncB9d — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 29, 2026

Retail and manufacturing hold the line

Retail trade gained 1.2% in August after contracting in July. Manufacturing rose 0.3%, its fifth increase in seven months, despite continued exposure to US tariffs. Construction added 0.2%.

Against those gains, utilities fell 0.4%, led by a 0.5% decline in electric power generation.

Public administration retreated as 2026 census preparation wound down. Mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction were flat.

What the shortfall means for December

Money markets are currently pricing in a hold at the Bank of Canada’s December 10 meeting, followed by a further 25-basis-point increase to 2.75% in January. Friday’s figures complicate that picture.

Marc Ercolao, economist at TD Economics, said the report missed in more than one direction.

“This was a disappointing report relative to expectations and, more importantly, Statistics Canada’s guidance for September looks no better,” he said.

“Taken together, that leaves real GDP growth in the third quarter tracking around 1.3% annualized — still positive, but notably below the Bank of Canada’s recent projection.”

For mortgage brokers monitoring what the BoC’s next decision means for the mortgage market and advising clients through an increasingly complex renewal environment, the gap between growth momentum and Bank projections has become a defining tension heading into year-end.

That concern sits alongside the broader unease felt across the industry since Canada’s rate hike deepened broker worry over a struggling housing market.

Ercolao went further on the Bank’s 2027 outlook.

“For the Bank of Canada, today’s report may cast a little more doubt around the durability of the recovery heading into 2027,” he said.

“The Bank’s latest outlook anticipates a meaningful strengthening in growth next year, but signs of softer momentum heading into Q4 raise the bar for that forecast, particularly with trade uncertainty and higher energy costs still clouding the outlook. While the Bank remains focused on upside inflation risks following this week’s rate hike, weaker underlying growth could complicate the case for further tightening in the near-term.”

The pattern echoes the two straight quarters of GDP contraction in the first half of 2026 that had brokers watching the Bank’s every move, and the second half of the year has yet to deliver the rebound either the Bank or the broker community had anticipated.

items.title: One Way to Make Toronto Condos More Livable: Let Buyers Make Them Bigger
items.description:
For years, Toronto developers built condos that were an easy sell to investors, even if they weren’t ideal places to live. But with the market reckoning with a glut of “shoebox” inventory, the shortcomings of that approach are tough to ignore. Purchasers want more space from their condos; they want room to actually live.

That’s been a takeaway from One Ten Avenue Road, a boutique condominium coming up at the southern edge of Midtown Toronto, where Yorkville meets The Annex. The building will be 12 storeys with just 72 private suites, and according to Managing Partner at Sierra Building Group Jeffrey Kansun, around 45% of purchasers have chosen to merge multiple units.

This is a central feature of Sierra’s “Crafted by You” program. It’s not unusual for pre-con buyers to be able to pick their finishings and fixtures, but at One Ten Ave. purchasers are also getting a say in size and layout.

Richard Wengle Architect Inc.

“It’s been a response to the market from day one. Not everyone’s wishes fit into a box, literally and figuratively,” says Kansun. “We developed this program in response to customers — we didn’t have this idea when we started this project.”

In the first six months of presales, Sierra didn’t sell a single unit smaller than 2,500 square feet. The buyers, Kansun says, tend to be later-career homeowners who want to trade the responsibilities of a large house for something more manageable — without sacrificing so much of the space they’re used to.

That said, the need for more space is something that transcends any one type of condo buyer. A recent analysis by proptech platform Wahi found that three- and four-plus-bedroom units have held their value much better than their smaller counterparts — even with sales down across all the board. While the median sale price of a one-bedroom condo in the GTA fell 14% between the first quarter of 2020 and the first quarter of 2026 (to $480,000), two-beds rose 2% (to $630,000), three-beds rose 13% (to $700,000), and four-plus-beds rose 15% (to $715,000).

“In today’s GTA condo market, the end user is the main source of anything resembling demand,” Wahi Economist Ryan McLaughlin said in the report. “There simply isn’t much appetite among buyers for smaller units, which have historically been geared primarily towards investors looking to flip them or rent them out.”

For Richard Wengle, founder of Richard Wengle Architect Inc. and the principal architect for One Ten Ave., designing for the end user has long been central to his work. Wengle’s firm has been working on projects that allow for this kind of customization since around 2011, starting with The Randall in Oakville. Since then, the firm has worked with purchasers at One Forest Hill and 89 Avenue Road (among others) to tailor layouts to their needs, including combining units to create larger, more personalized homes.

For One Ten Ave., the “typical wish-list” for units that are being combined includes things like a large kitchen and dining room, generous closet space and extra storage, and a larger patio space than you would see attached to a Toronto-area condo. These are the kinds of features that purchasers — Wengle calls them “right-sizers” — are usually giving up when moving from a home to a condo.

And then there are other requests that require a more inventive architectural approach. “One purchaser is taking one floor and part of the floor below, where they'll have a separate private section that might be for kids that come to visit,” says Wengle. “So they're not necessarily walking through space that's not being used all the time and feeling like it's wasted.”

Of course, there are limits to the program. Plumbing and mechanical stacks, elevators, corridors, and structural elements are fixed, but non-load-bearing walls can often be moved to create a layout that better suits the owner. The goal is to work within those constraints while making the most of a unit’s views, natural light, and access to outdoor space.

For now, this kind of customization remains easier to offer in the luxury market, where buyers have the budgets to purchase additional square footage and manage the costs of the architectural services and — because customized layouts require more oversight and coordination to execute — higher construction management costs for the developer. But Kansun hopes the principle behind the approach is something that will catch on in the broader pre-con condo market.

“A lot of developers stuck with very small, un-livable units, and the values have just plummeted because of it. And the unfortunate reality is that it makes sense — you can’t really sell a unit that you can’t live in,” he says. “We, as an industry, will hopefully not make the same mistake twice.”

items._ogDesc: The CMHC forecasts Canadian mortgage arrears will hit a 9-year high by 2027. Here is why the national housing agency might be underestimating the fallout.
items.body:
Canada’s national housing agency is bearish on real estate over the near term. The CMHC’s latest forecast shows Canadian Bankers Association (CBA) mortgage arrears climbing into 2027. The trend is driven almost entirely by a surge in Ontario. That suggests they might be underestimating the fallout, since home prices in other provinces are only just starting to correct.

Canadian Mortgage Arrears Have Climbed Aggressively

The arrears rate at Canada’s banks is on an aggressive climb. The share of mortgages in arrears hit 0.29% in July, up 6 basis points (bps) from last year. That’s the highest rate since 2015, more than doubling from the record low less than 5 years ago. It isn’t over either.

Canadian Mortgage Arrears Forecast To Keep Climbing

Canadian mortgage arrears rate (90 days past due) and CMHC forecast.

Source: CBA; CMHC; Better Dwelling.

The CMHC forecasts the arrears rate will continue to rise through mid-2027. They expect it to hit 0.33% by February and hold there through June 2027, the end of the forecast period. That would push arrears to the highest level since 2012.

Why The CMHC Might Be Underestimating Arrears

A closer look at the forecast reveals the agency might be underestimating the stress. The projection is primarily driven by a 58% surge in arrears in Ontario, one of 2 provinces ending the forecast at a cycle high. Slow real estate sales, a rocky job market, and a price correction are cited as the drivers. However, they’re missing a key detail—other provinces haven’t seen a correction yet.

Canadian home prices made a substantial correction after most markets slipped in 2022. However, Ontario and BC are the only provinces to see a major correction, and only the former’s drop is bigger than the national average. Despite prices across the country getting a massive lift from the low-rate boom, all but 2 remain just off record highs. Slow sales are lingering as a result of market inefficiencies that still need to correct.

These provinces don’t appear to be immune to gravity, though. Last month, prices in regions that largely resisted the correction began making near-record declines. The declines have only just started in most of the country, potentially spreading Ontario’s climate to more markets. That would prove to be a major headwind for arrears in those regions.

items.title: B.C. investors turn to retail plazas amid tight supply: report
items.description: Metro Vancouver retail vacancy falls below 1% in some areas: Re/Max
items._ogDesc: Metro Vancouver retail vacancy falls below 1% in some areas: Re/Max
items.body:
Neighbourhood retail vacancy has fallen below one per cent in some Metro Vancouver suburbs as investors turn to established properties, according to a new report.

The Re/Max Canada Fall 2026 Commercial Real Estate Report, released Thursday, found that retail vacancy had fallen below three per cent in downtown Vancouver and less than one per cent in some suburban neighbourhoods.

Conditions across B.C. remain uneven as some other markets, including Kelowna, has been more subdued with limited new building supply weighing on rental conditions and higher costs slowing development, the report said.

“Supply has become increasingly constrained in some of the country’s key commercial markets,” said Don Kottick, president of Re/Max Canada.

Commercial real estate investors in B.C. are favouring neighbourhood retail plazas and existing industrial properties, as demand for well-located space remains strong. Meanwhile, high construction and financing costs are weighing on new development, according to the report.

“We've seen considerable investment in established, income-producing properties this year, particularly in markets where demand remains strong,” said Kristie Kimnach, executive director of Re/Max Commercial, in a statement.

“The challenge in some of these markets seems to have been finding enough quality products to meet investor demand.”

Neighbourhood shopping plazas and grocery-anchored centres have attracted tenants in sectors including medical services, health, wellness, beauty and food services, the report said.

However, strong demand for industrial space has not necessarily translated into higher sale prices in Greater Vancouver. Industrial sale prices softened even as availability tightened, according to the report.

Kottick said the imbalance between strong demand for established retail space—particularly smaller units in high-demand markets—and a lack of new developments could persist amid higher bond yields and economic uncertainty.

Nationally, 11 of the 12 markets examined reported improving industrial market conditions, measured by increasing absorption and decreasing availability. Retail conditions improved in 10 markets, while multi-family improved in seven markets.

Looking ahead to 2027, Re/Max anticipates a gradual and uneven recovery in Canada's commercial real estate market.

“While demand for established, income-producing properties is expected to remain strong, limited new construction could create further supply challenges in markets where demand continues to grow,” the report said.

The report draws on data and insights from Re/Max brokers and agents across 12 major Canadian markets, comparing activity from January to June 2026 with the same period a year earlier.

items.title: Is homeownership becoming out of reach for young Canadians?
items.description: A new Zown survey maps the financial barriers standing between young Canadians and homeownership
items.content: <p>A new Zown survey maps the financial barriers standing between young Canadians and homeownership</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0356_639289595409033941.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: A new Zown survey maps the financial barriers standing between young Canadians and homeownership
items.body:
For many young Canadians, the aspiration to own a home is not in doubt. What is increasingly uncertain is whether the financial foundations are there to support it.

A new survey puts those anxieties in sharp relief. Conducted by Toronto-based AI-powered real estate brokerage Zown and the Angus Reid Forum between October 14 and October 16, 2026, the 2026 Zown Homeownership & Financial Confidence Survey polled 1,500 adult Canadians.

It found that 82% of respondents aged 18 to 34 lacked confidence in at least one financial aspect of the homebuying process. That compares with 35% of those aged 35 to 54 and 50% of Canadians 55 and older who felt fully confident across the board.

Only 18% of those in the youngest cohort said they felt equipped to handle every financial dimension of a purchase.

Young buyers named saving and planning for a down payment (19%) and understanding ongoing ownership costs (19%) as the weakest points, followed by knowing how much home they could afford (18%), awareness of government incentives and programmes (14%), and calculating closing costs (10%).

Areas of lowest confidence — Canadians aged 18–34

% who identified this as an area of low confidence

Areas of lowest confidence — prospective buyers who have never owned

Source: 2026 Zown Homeownership & Financial Confidence Survey — Zown / Angus Reid Forum — 1,500 adult Canadians — October 14–16, 2026 — margin of error ±2.53 percentage points, 19 times out of 20

Savings drawn down to meet everyday costs

Some 40% of Canadians dipped into long-term savings over the past year to cover ordinary expenses — 29% for emergencies, 22% for groceries and everyday purchases, and 13% for regular housing costs including rent or mortgage payments.

As Canadian Mortgage Professional’s reporting on Canada’s housing affordability challenges facing mortgage shoppers has shown, improving macro-level conditions in prices and rates have yet to relieve household-level financial strain.

Alberta led regionally at 48%, followed by Saskatchewan and Manitoba at 44% combined, Ontario and British Columbia at 41% each, Atlantic Canada at 35%, and Quebec at 34%.

“Housing affordability isn’t just about the price of a home. It’s also about whether Canadians can afford to become homeowners in the first place,” said Rishard Rameez, founder and chief executive officer of Zown, in Toronto.

“We’re asking people to save tens of thousands of dollars for a down payment when they’re already drawing on their savings to cover everyday expenses. That’s a fundamental challenge we can’t afford to overlook.”

Chris Allard of Smart Debt Mortgages says many borrowers are focusing on their personal finances and affordability rather than trying to predict the next twist in trade tensions or interest rates. https://t.co/lFVdypu2V5 — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 27, 2026

What brokers can offer underprepared clients

The confidence gap is steepest among those with no ownership history: only 13% of Canadians who have never owned a home but haven’t ruled it out say they feel prepared across all financial aspects, versus 46% of current homeowners.

Christa Tessier, broker and co-owner of Mortgage Advisors, previously told CMP that limited savings and elevated debt-to-income ratios are leaving many clients unable to qualify under standard lender requirements.

“Borrowers should focus on reducing debt as much as possible and maintaining good credit habits such as paying bills on time and keeping credit utilization low,” she said.

“Saving diligently for a down payment, closing costs, and a financial cushion can make a significant difference.”

Brokers who invest in that preparation work are starting to see results. Sarita Free, a mortgage agent with Mortgage Powered Financial Group in Norfolk County, Ontario, told CMP that 2025 and 2026 had been a turning point for buyers who had long been frozen out.

“A lot of my clients are first-time homebuyers and they’ve finally been able to break in,” she said.

“This year, I’m finding that they’re finally able to get into the market. With the 30-year amortization that we can now go to, I find a lot of my buyers that have been on the sidelines are finally able to… stay in their hometown where they’ve grown up, and not have to go elsewhere.”

The post Ontario Mortgage Arrears To Keep Surging, Led by Toronto: CMHC appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Ontario mortgage arrears are nearing 2008 levels, with Toronto leading the stress. CMHC expects arrears to keep rising through mid-2027.
items.body:
The Ontario real estate downturn is expected to worsen. Mortgage arrears in the province are approaching 2008 levels, according to the CMHC. The risk is even further amplified in Greater Toronto, especially with private lenders. The agency warns Ontario’s sharpest and most persistent surge in arrears will persist through mid-2027.

Ontario’s Real Estate Boom and Bust

Ontario was the center of Canada’s real estate bubble and now it’s the center of its bust. The low rate frenzy sent prices 64% (+$393.6k) higher between April 2020 and March 2022. Since then, prices have dropped 26.7% (-$268.8k), reversing most gains—but not all. That little nugget is important when it comes to making sense of the arrears data we’ll get to soon. But first, let’s make sure we’re all on the same page when it comes to mortgage arrears.

The industry tends to frame rising arrears as a hard-hit consumer problem. In reality, households are hard hit during good times too. When someone can’t pay their mortgage, they typically try to sell. In a market boom, they sell pretty fast and feel like a genius when those profits flow in. When there’s a downturn, it takes longer to sell and not doing it fast enough means they end up in arrears. However, every property has a buyer—it’s a matter of price.

Would you rather go into arrears or lower your price? Obviously, the latter, which suggests those who don’t can’t actually do that. That’s mostly peak buyers, who in many cases see their equity wiped out entirely, and have to pay to sell. Ontario’s boom and bust is concentrated around investor-dominated Greater Toronto. CMHC doesn’t break down arrears by investors versus owner-occupiers, but the US housing crash provides some insight. Their downturn during the financial crisis is often blamed on overleveraged households, but the data shows it was an investor crash. Investors were just tapping subprime lenders to get more leverage.

Now that we have clear, let’s talk about arrears.

Ontario Mortgage Stress Builds, Private Lender Arrears Surge

Residential mortgage arrears rate at mortgage investment entities (MIEs): Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area (GTHA) vs Rest of Canada.

Source: CMHC; Better Dwelling.

Ontario has seen a surge in mortgage arrears. The arrears rate at CBA member banks hit 0.32% in Q2 2026, up 52% from a year before and over 5x the low in Q2 2022. The downturn is concentrated in the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area (GTHA) and Southwestern Ontario, says the CMHC.

CBA data understates the scale of the problem since it excludes roughly 1 in 5 mortgages. As previously noted, banks tend to sell or not renew underperforming or riskier loans. Those borrowers often end up at mortgage investment entities (MIEs), along with a clientele that can’t obtain traditional financing. MIEs have seen the arrears rate explode around the GTHA from 3.0% in Q3 2023 to 11.1% in Q1 2026. These lenders represent only 1.8% of outstanding mortgage balances nationally, but their GTHA arrears rate is over three times the national rate.

“Although MIEs account for a small share of the mortgage market, GTHA MIE arrears could provide an early signal of broader mortgage market stress,” explains the CMHC.

Ontario Mortgage Arrears Forecast To Rise Through Mid-2027

Ontario CBA mortgage arrears rate and CMHC forecast.

Source: CBA; CMHC; Better Dwelling.

The worst is yet to come, according to the CMHC. Even after the renewal shock, the agency expects a further erosion in credit quality in the province. They warn that the arrears rate in Ontario is expected to climb through mid-2027, with Toronto being primarily exposed.

“Ontario is projected to record the largest and most sustained increase in mortgage arrears, concentrated in the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area (GTHA) and Southwestern Ontario,” warns the CMHC.

Ontario isn’t alone in the potential worsening, but high prices and a concentration of trade tensions increase sensitivity. The agency specifically cites trade tensions threatening manufacturing employment, while weak resale conditions make it harder for stressed borrowers to exit.

items.title: Canadian Mortgage Awards return for a landmark 20th year

items.content: <p>The 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards arrive November 25 with 23 categories and a milestone to mark</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639288966737284341.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: The 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards arrive November 25 with 23 categories and a milestone to mark
items.body:
On November 25, hundreds of Canada's mortgage brokers, lenders, and industry leaders will gather at Rebel Toronto for an evening that now spans two decades.

The 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards (CMAs), presented by Canadian Mortgage Professional, will recognise outstanding work across 23 competitive categories, from broker specialists in private lending and reverse mortgages to the teams and technology companies reshaping the industry.

For the professionals shortlisted this year, the wait is almost over.

The night ahead

The evening begins at 6:00 p.m. with a cocktail reception on the first floor of Rebel Toronto, the waterfront event space at 11 Polson Street.

For an industry that spent much of 2025 navigating a historically concentrated wave of mortgage renewals, the reception offers something rarer: two hours to simply connect.

Guests are encouraged to arrive promptly, with the awards ceremony and dinner banquet commencing at 7:30 p.m.

The post-awards celebration runs from 10:30 p.m. onwards, giving the night room to breathe well past the final announcement.

The 2026 host is Sonia Mangat, a broadcaster and storyteller with a decade of experience across news, entertainment, and live event hosting in Canada.

Mangat currently appears on eTalk and CP24 Breakfast and has hosted high-profile stages including the Canadian Screen Awards.

As a skilled interviewer who has sat down with A-list celebrities, she brings the kind of relaxed authority a room of mortgage professionals tends to respond to – someone who commands attention without demanding deference.

Entertainment for the evening includes Soulfire, a five-piece live band specialising in classic rock, soul, Motown, disco, and Top 40 hits.

The dress code is formal: tuxedo, business suit, long gown, cocktail dress, or traditional attire. For those seeking a rental, the event has partnered with The Fitzroy Dress Rental, offering a 10 per cent discount with the code CMA26.

Secure a table at the 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards and celebrate your team’s achievements alongside industry leaders, innovators, and top-performing professionals from across the country. #MortgageAwardsCA Book your table today: https://t.co/SSKx4yuft5 https://t.co/f31Lgyrrzt — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 28, 2026

Voices from past ceremonies

For Akshay Gupta, a commercial real estate mortgage agent at Foundry Mortgage Capital Corp. in Toronto and the 2025 Young Achiever of the Year, the CMA win carried practical weight beyond the gala night itself.

"Developers and investors need confidence in their advisor from day one," Gupta said.

"The CMA win signals that the work has been independently validated at a national level, which opens doors and shortens the trust-building process in a way that's otherwise difficult to manufacture."

Dalia Barsoum of Streetwise Mortgages, who took out both the Ontario and national Broker of the Year awards at the 2024 edition, pointed to what the recognition meant in a market that had just come through a difficult year.

"Especially as 2023 was a very challenging year in the industry, this award has a very special meaning right now," Barsoum said.

"Creative solutions for clients, really pushing through tough files, helping my team ride the wave and sticking together as a team were some things that I believe we did really well this year."

The spirit of community that runs through the awards was articulated at the 2024 gala by Carey Benvenuti of Lending Niagara – Mortgage Architects, who won the philanthropy category.

"The gift of giving is the gift that you give yourself," Benvenuti said.

Joe White, chief executive officer at the Real Estate and Mortgage Institute of Canada (REMIC) in Toronto, which sponsors the Broker of the Year award, captured the purpose of the evening plainly: "This award is the cream of the crop. It's something the industry needs to embrace and joyfully talk about – those helping Canadians with homeownership and financial freedom."

A milestone moment for the industry

The 2026 CMAs mark the programme's 20th anniversary – a milestone that coincides with one of the most structurally consequential periods in the Canadian mortgage market's recent history. 

Shawn Allen, founder of Matrix Mortgage Global and a past CMA sponsor, has spoken about the role these gatherings play after periods of industry stress.

"The industry went through a hard time with COVID, and now we need to show solidarity," Allen said.

"These awards are about giving back and celebrating achievements." That instinct – to mark what the industry has built and who has built it well – is what twenty years of Canadian Mortgage Awards have institutionalised.

The 2026 programme spans 26 categories in total, including the Haventree Bank Award for Lifetime Achievement, which carries no nominated finalists and is announced only on the night.

Sponsors backing the programme include CMI Canadian Mortgages Inc., Equitable Bank, Haventree Bank, MCAN Mortgage Corporation, RFA Mortgage Corporation, and Real Property Solutions Inc. (RPS).

Winners will be revealed live at Rebel Toronto on November 25 and published the same night across CMP's channels.

Registration for the November 25 gala is open at canadianmortgageawards.com.

items.title: Equitable Bank to sell Bennington Financial to Desjardins Group
items.description: EQB offloads its equipment leasing arm to Desjardins as it sharpens focus on core growth
items.content: <p>EQB offloads its equipment leasing arm to Desjardins as it sharpens focus on core growth</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639288916419378197.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: EQB offloads its equipment leasing arm to Desjardins as it sharpens focus on core growth
items.body:
Equitable Bank, the Toronto-based lender that routes its alternative mortgages exclusively through Canada’s broker channel, has agreed to sell its commercial equipment leasing subsidiary, Bennington Financial Corp., to Desjardins Group.

The deal marks another step in EQB Inc.’s deliberate exit from non-core businesses. It follows their acquisition of PC Financial, which closed in July and added nearly four million customers.

Desjardins Group will acquire 100% of Bennington’s shares at a price equivalent to an approximately 8% discount to lease receivables.

As at July 31, Bennington’s aggregate portfolio held roughly $1.1 billion in lease receivables. The transaction is expected to close in the first half of 2027. 

EQB will reclassify Bennington as held for sale and record a net after-tax charge in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, treated as an adjusting item.

The deal is expected to be relatively neutral to Equitable Bank’s common equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital ratio at closing.

Chadwick Westlake, President and Chief Executive Officer of EQB Inc. in Toronto, Ontario, said the divestiture is a natural extension of the bank’s recalibrated priorities.

“At EQB, we’re focused on doing more of what we do best and investing where we see the greatest opportunity to win,” he said.

“This transaction allows us to further concentrate our capital and resources on our core growth priorities, particularly following our PC Financial transaction. It also positions Bennington with an owner that is equipped to grow the business to its full potential with expertise in the sector. Consistent with other businesses and product exits over the past year, this move strengthens our ability to create value for customers and shareholders over the long term.”

A pattern of deliberate portfolio exits

The Bennington sale continues a visible pivot at EQB. Since completing the acquisition of PC Financial, EQB has moved steadily to shed businesses that no longer align with its core focus.

Canadian Mortgage Professional has followed EQB’s most profitable year on record, when annual revenue surpassed $1 billion for the first time in fiscal 2025.

The broker channel remains central to that model; as one Equitable Bank executive previously confirmed to Canadian Mortgage Professional, “We continue to believe that the best way in this country to get a mortgage is through a mortgage broker.”

A strategic fit for Desjardins

Denis Dubois, President and CEO of Desjardins Group in Lévis, Québec, said the deal complements the cooperative’s existing business financing capabilities.

“Bennington’s specialized expertise in commercial equipment leasing and financing makes it a strong strategic fit for Desjardins,” he said.

“This transaction brings capabilities that complement our existing business financing offering and support our growth ambitions across Canada, while providing a strong foundation for Bennington to continue building on its established business, expertise and relationships.”

Desjardins Group is a financial cooperative, offering personal and business banking, wealth management, and insurance services to more than 10 million members and clients, with total net revenue of $16.31 billion and total assets of $510.2 billion in fiscal 2025.

National Bank Capital Markets and McCarthy Tétrault LLP are advising EQB on the transaction. Desjardins Capital Markets and Norton Rose Fulbright Canada LLP are advising Desjardins.

items.description: Variable-rate mortgage and HELOC borrowers face higher costs today as Canada’s big six banks move
items.content: <p>Variable-rate mortgage and HELOC borrowers face higher costs today as Canada’s big six banks move</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639288897773939059.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Variable-rate mortgage and HELOC borrowers face higher costs today as Canada’s big six banks move
items.body:
Canada’s variable-rate mortgage holders and home equity line of credit (HELOC) borrowers are paying more as of today, after the country’s six largest banks put a new prime lending rate of 4.70% into effect. 

The move follows the Bank of Canada’s (BoC) decision to raise its overnight rate by 25 basis points to 2.50% on Wednesday, its first increase since 2023.

The Royal Bank of Canada (RBC), Toronto-Dominion Bank (TD), Bank of Montreal (BMO), Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce (CIBC), Bank of Nova Scotia (Scotiabank), and National Bank of Canada each implemented the quarter-point increase, moving in lockstep from a prime rate of 4.45% that had been in place since October 2025.

TD also raised its separate mortgage prime rate — the benchmark used to price its variable-rate mortgage products — to 4.85% from 4.60%, a spread that sits 15 basis points above its standard prime.

For borrowers on fixed-payment variable mortgages, today’s change means a larger share of each instalment goes toward interest rather than principal. Those on adjustable-payment structures will see monthly costs rise immediately.

A housing market that wasn’t moving before today

The effective rate increase reaches a market that had already gone quiet.

Phil Soper, president and chief executive of Royal LePage in Toronto, told Canadian Mortgage Professional this month that anticipated buyer pull-ahead had not materialised even as rate-hike speculation intensified.

“You’d see some people that were planning to get into the market in the spring of 2027, for example, jumping in now to get ahead of anticipated higher borrowing costs. Yet we’re not seeing material changes in the trajectory of transaction volumes. It’s very flat,” Soper said.

Benjamin Reitzes of BMO says the Bank of Canada's first rate hike in more than three years may not be its last, with future decisions likely hinging on economic growth, inflation trends, and incoming data over the months ahead. https://t.co/lcW0HncB9d — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 29, 2026

What brokers need to tell clients today

Leah Zlatkin, mortgage broker and expert at LowestRates.ca, said in April that borrower psychology still carries heavy residue from the previous hiking cycle.

“Most borrowers still prefer the certainty of fixed payments, especially after the sharp increases to variable rates during the Bank of Canada’s rate-hiking cycle in 2022 and 2023,” Zlatkin said. That hesitancy only deepens with today’s move confirmed.

“Variable rates come with uncertainty,” she added. “Borrowers need to be comfortable with the possibility that rates could move higher again depending on how the economic environment evolves.”

Victor Tran, spokesperson at Rates.ca, shared earlier this year that despite growing curiosity around variable products, fixed-rate mortgages still dominate client decisions.

“Most households are still opting for fixed because it offers predictability in an environment where rate direction isn’t guaranteed,” Tran said.

items.title: Award-Winning Flemingdon Park Office-Turned-Rental Makes A Case For Conversions
items.description:
Located in Toronto’s Flemingdon Park neighbourhood, e-lofts — a 15-storey office-to-residential conversion project — has won a coveted Ontario Home Builders’ Association (OHBA) award in its final months of construction.

The purpose-built rental development, which was first proposed in spring 2025, was awarded High-Rise Building of the Year at the OHBA’s 2026 Awards of Distinction Gala for “outstanding architecture, innovation, and design excellence,” according to a press release from the project’s developer, Amexon Developments. The win is significant given the low number of adaptive reuse projects in the province.

Office-to-residential conversion was an idea that picked up speed at the tail end of the pandemic, when a record-high number of office buildings were sitting vacant, and more housing was desperately needed. Why not turn those vacant offices into apartments or condos?

Turns out, it’s a bit more complex than that. In Toronto, older office buildings tend to have physical characteristics that don’t support residential layouts. For example, offices often have deep floorplates that restrict sunlight from reaching the centre of the building, or they have too few elevators or insufficient plumbing capacity — all costly deficiencies that make demolitions more attractive by comparison.

Meanwhile, red tape, like Toronto’s office replacement requirements, and a lack of municipal grants, such as Calgary’s Downtown Office Conversion Program — which offers up to $75 per square foot for qualifying adaptive re-use projects — limit the financial and logistical viability of such retrofits.

Amexon’s e-lofts, however, is one of the exceptions. “Not all buildings are suitable for conversion — this one is exceptional because it has all the right attributes to support a successful conversion into residential lofts,” says Ashling Evans, vice president of real estate at Amexon Developments. “With over 300,000 sq. ft of buildable area, infrastructure costs can be efficiently distributed across 331 units.” In comparison, smaller buildings in the 100,000–200,000 sq.-ft-range often lack the economies of scale to make conversion financially viable.

e-lofts exterior

e-lofts fitness centre

On top of sheer size, the former Flemingdon Park office building’s design made an optimal foundation for residential living. “A centrally-located elevator core allows for optimal unit planning,” says Evans. “In contrast, many office buildings have off-centre cores that limit layout flexibility and make residential conversion inefficient or impossible.”

Aside from the challenging removal of the large, heavy precast exterior walls to allow for larger residential windows, Amexon sees the building’s commercial past as an advantage.

“The adaptive reuse approach takes advantage of the building’s existing structure to deliver housing faster and more sustainably than ground-up construction,” says Evans. It has been a speedy project, with occupancy expected in summer 2027, just over two years after the initial building application was filed. “Also, the loft-style suites at e-lofts will feature 12-foot floor-to-ceiling windows, polished concrete floors, exposed spiral ductwork, and structural elements for an industrial-chic aesthetic,” she adds.

Another integral aspect of the retrofit is a whole host of eco-friendly updates, including carbon-free mechanical systems that improve air quality and efficiency, green roofs and rainwater harvesting systems, and EV charging stations installed at every parking space.

e-lofts coworking space

Also available to residents will be an array of amenities. This includes a fitness centre, co-working spaces, pet daycare, and a 12,000-sq.-ft. rooftop patio with a saltwater pool, lounge areas, communal herb garden, and outdoor fitness zones.

While office-to-residential conversions haven’t taken off the way it once seemed they would, e-lofts serves as a rare example that, when physical design and financial logistics align, commercial spaces can be given new life.

items.description: The Bank of Canada's rate hike Wednesday is set to translate to higher borrowing costs for homebuyers, adding further pressure as the real estate sector also copes with rising prices for construction materials.
items._ogDesc: The Bank of Canada's rate hike Wednesday is set to translate to higher borrowing costs for homebuyers, adding further pressure as the real estate sector also copes with rising prices for construction materials.
items.body:
The Bank of Canada's rate hike Wednesday is set to translate to higher borrowing costs for homebuyers, adding further pressure as the real estate sector also copes with rising prices for construction materials.

The central bank raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter-point to 2.5 per cent, the first increase in more than three years, as it warned that inflation driven by the war in the Middle East is likely to spread.

"There's a number of things weighing on housing right now," the bank's senior deputy governor Carolyn Rogers told reporters, as she described a "subdued" outlook for the sector.

"Certainly, borrowing rates are currently weighing a bit on the housing market. An increase will add to that a bit on the margin, so I think the outlook we've got for housing in the forecast here takes all of that into account."

The big question is whether the central bank's move is a one-time adjustment or the start of a sustained tightening cycle, said Phil Soper, president and CEO of real estate firm Royal LePage.

He said the sector's "prolonged weakness is already weighing on economic growth, and higher borrowing costs will only deepen that challenge."

Shawn Zigelstein, a broker for Royal LePage Signature Realty, said he believes the rate hike won't have a major effect on consumer confidence just yet.

"It's not like we are in a market like we were back in 2022 where the prices are increasing substantially on a regular basis," he said in an interview.

"A quarter-point adjustment really shouldn't make too much of a difference on someone's mortgage payments at this point."

The central bank's key policy rate had held steady for nearly a year following a series of cuts. Inflation ticked up to 3.1 per cent in September due to high gas prices, and the bank said an increase to the rate is necessary to reduce the risk that elevated energy prices spill over to other goods and services.

Zigelstein said clients he speaks with are more concerned about other day-to-day costs and whether the overall inflation environment makes it the right time to buy a home.

"They have been worried about other factors, including tariffs and such. Are they going to have the jobs that they had? Are their investments going to do what they've been doing? So they've got bigger concerns than worrying about interest rates," he said.

"Now, of course, if the rates start to change a little bit, then we will start to see potentially a little bit of a pullback on what people are spending because borrowing costs will be higher."

While Canada "is not facing a broad mortgage crisis," there are signs of financial pressure concentrated in specific regions such as the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area and southwestern Ontario, said Aled ab Iorwerth, deputy chief economist for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp., earlier this week.

He said trade tensions are weighing on key manufacturing sectors such as the automotive industry in those areas, leading to labour-market uncertainty and softer housing market conditions.

CMHC said Ontario's mortgage arrears rate reached 0.32 per cent in the second quarter, which is still below historical peaks but expected to continue rising through mid-2027. British Columbia and Atlantic Canada are expected to see a more moderate rise in mortgage arrears over the same period.

"The mortgage system is adjusting, but these early warning signs, particularly in parts of Ontario, need to be monitored closely," ab Iorwerth said in a news release.

Don Kottick, president of Re/Max Canada, said that while an interest-rate increase "may give some buyers pause," more balanced market conditions in many regions are creating opportunities for buyers, including greater choice and room to negotiate.

In September, the national average sale price fell 1.6 per cent year-over-year to $666,538, according to the Canadian Real Estate Association. National home sales were down 7.7 per cent from the same month last year, as the association cited higher fixed mortgage rates and the Bank of Canada's "notably more hawkish tone."

Fixed rates are largely unaffected by the Bank of Canada's decision, having already moved higher in recent months in line with the bond market. But further movement in the bond market into 2027 could prompt mortgage costs to jump, which "would have a dampening impact on home purchases," said Michael Waters, CEO of Minto Group, a real estate developer.

"Higher rates, everything else held equal, will reduce levels of purchaser activity for anything durable of size — cars and houses, certainly," Waters said in an interview.

"The housing sector is very slow right now and so that obviously would be a concern for anyone in that sector."

Meanwhile, the central bank said Wednesday that higher energy and import costs are expected to raise the costs of housing construction and maintenance through higher prices for materials and equipment.

Any increase to the cost of credit will also have an effect on the ability to build new projects, particularly new housing and supporting infrastructure, said Nicole Emmett, vice-president of communications, marketing and member services for the Canadian Construction Association.

"A home isn’t a home without the roads, sewers and watermains that support it, and higher borrowing costs put pressure on the margins of the contractors building them, which are already stretched by global supply chain disruptions and material costs," she said in a statement.

"Many contractors also rely on financing for equipment, materials and day-to-day operations."

Waters said higher interest — construction loans are based on a floating rate — along with rising input costs "will squeeze margins" and potentially lead to fewer large-scale project completions in the coming years.

"Certainly projects are far more challenged today than they would have been six months ago, pre-Iran war," he said.

"The impact would be fewer projects meeting economic feasibility tests and more projects probably sitting idle until market conditions improve, so that could have a negative impact on the creation of new housing supply."

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 28, 2026.

Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press

The post Bank of Canada Sees Elevated Inflation Into 2028, Housing To Remain Weak appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.5%, forecasting elevated inflation into 2028 as higher costs keep housing activity weak and push shelter inflation higher.
items.body:
Canada’s central bank raised its key policy rate as it tries to tame rising inflation. The Bank of Canada (BoC) hiked its overnight rate 25 basis points to 2.5% this morning, its first hike in over 3 years. In the accompanying report, the BoC warns of elevated inflation into mid-2028. Higher input and financing costs will also keep housing activity weak while boosting shelter inflation.

Canadian Inflation Isn’t Expected To Return To Target Until 2028

The BoC sees elevated inflation into 2028. The latest forecast from the central bank shows CPI inflation above 3% through Q3 2027. That’s roughly a point higher than they anticipated in their July report. It isn’t expected to return to their 2% target rate until mid-2028. While elevated inflation has largely been confined to energy and related categories, the Bank expects those pressures to spread over the next year.

High energy prices are spreading into production, transportation, and imports. Businesses have absorbed much of the increase so far, but expect to pass more on to consumers over the next 12 months, warns the BoC. Even after energy inflation turns negative in late 2027, earlier cost increases will continue to work their way through supply chains and boost prices.

Source: Bank of Canada.

Canadian Housing Investment Forecast To Lag The Economy

Higher rates are seen putting a drag on one of the country’s biggest components of GDP—housing investment. Residential investment primarily consists of spending on new home construction and substantial renovation. This sector is seen averaging less than 1% growth in 2027 and 2028. In contrast, GDP growth is expected to be roughly 2% for both years. The whole economy isn’t expected to slow, but housing will underperform.

Weak demand and high input costs are the reasons they cite. A lack of affordability, slow population growth, and rising borrowing costs are seen hitting the brakes on the demand side. Meanwhile, higher energy costs and imported input costs will make construction more expensive, throttling building activity.

Weak Housing Activity Isn’t Expected To Slow Rising Shelter Costs

Weak housing investment isn’t expected to slow shelter service inflation. It’s forecast to rise from just over 1% at the end of 2026 to 2% in 2027, and remain near that level into 2028. Higher material, equipment, construction, and maintenance costs are seen as the primary driver. Rising borrowing costs are expected to add further upward pressure. Rent inflation is seen as one of the few moderating factors for shelter, but it only partially offsets the other factors.

The impact on home prices isn’t clear, but higher expenses and weak demand aren’t bullish. At the same time, weak activity doesn’t automatically lead to affordability improvements.

The BoC report leaves an inflationary issue untouched: how government-backed construction spending supports higher input costs. Large projects compete for workers, resources, equipment, and land—even as private housing demand weakens. That spending can limit the disinflationary relief normally associated with a slowdown, leaving input costs elevated despite weak qualified demand.

items.title: Only 18% Of Young Canadians Fully Confident About Homebuying Finances: Survey
items.description:
Just 18% of Canadians aged 18 to 34 say they feel confident navigating all financial aspects of buying a home, according to the 2026 Zown Homeownership & Financial Confidence Survey, released Wednesday.

That compares with 35% of those aged 35 to 54 and 50% of those 55 and older.

Zown, an AI-powered real estate brokerage, conducted the survey from October 14 to 16 among 1,500 online adult Canadians who are members of the Angus Reid Forum.

The survey also found 40% of Canadians tapped into their long-term savings over the past year to cover expenses or unexpected costs.

Among those who did, 29% used the money for emergencies or unexpected expenses, and 22% for groceries and everyday purchases. Another 13% put it toward regular housing costs, including rent or mortgage payments.

Alberta had the highest share of respondents drawing on long-term savings, at 48%. Saskatchewan and Manitoba combined came in at 44%, followed by Ontario and British Columbia at 41% each, Atlantic Canada at 35%, and Quebec at 34%.

“Housing affordability isn’t just about the price of a home. It’s also about whether Canadians can afford to become homeowners in the first place,” said Rishard Rameez, founder and CEO of Zown.

“There’s a disconnect between the dream of homeownership and the financial reality many Canadians face. We’re asking people to save tens of thousands of dollars for a down payment when they’re already drawing on their savings to cover everyday expenses. That’s a fundamental challenge we can’t afford to overlook.”

For the younger group, saving and planning for a downpayment and understanding the ongoing costs after buying a home were the areas of least confidence, at 19% each. Knowing how much home they can afford came next at 18%, then knowing which homebuying incentives or programs they qualify for (14%) and understanding closing costs (10%).

Ownership makes a similar difference. Only 13% of Canadians who have never owned a home, but haven’t ruled it out, feel confident across every financial aspect of buying one, compared with 46% of current homeowners.

For those prospective buyers, the downpayment is the area of least confidence, cited by 30%. Understanding how much home they can afford follows at 18%, and the ongoing costs of homeownership at 14%.

items.title: Bank Of Canada Raises Policy Rate To 2.5% In First Hike Since 2023
items.description:
The Bank of Canada raised its target for the overnight rate by 25 basis points on Wednesday, bringing it to 2.5% and marking the first increase since July 0f 2023.

The Bank Rate now sits at 2.75%, and the deposit rate at 2.45%.

Inflation is running higher and longer than the Bank projected in July. CPI inflation has hovered around 3% since April, and the Bank expects it to climb to about 3.5% by the end of the year, largely because of persistently high oil prices.

Take gasoline out and the numbers look calmer. Inflation excluding gas was 2.2% in September, and core measures remain close to 2%. The Bank is more worried about where costs are heading. High fuel prices are raising production and transportation costs, imported industrial and electronics inputs have become more expensive, and Bank surveys suggest businesses will pass more of those costs on to customers over the next year.

The conflict in the Middle East is now in its eighth month with no clear path to resolution. The Bank expects CPI inflation to average 3% in 2027, a full percentage point above its July projection, before easing to 2% in the middle of 2028.

Governing Council said the hike is meant to reduce the risk that high energy prices spread into the prices of other goods and services. It said further increases may be needed, but that it would proceed carefully given the uncertainty.

The economy has outperformed expectations. GDP grew 3.3% in the second quarter, and recent indicators point to about 2% growth in the third, both stronger than the Bank anticipated. Consumer spending held up despite slow population growth, and business investment rebounded on oil and gas activity and machinery and equipment spending. Unemployment has held around 6.5% for several months.

New US tariffs are expected to slow growth in the fourth quarter. The Bank projects the economy will grow 1% in 2026 and 2% in both 2027 and 2028, a somewhat stronger outlook than July’s, though Canada-US trade relations remain a major source of uncertainty.

Business investment, exports and fiscal measures are expected to drive the 2027 rebound. Housing, however, isn’t on that list. The Bank expects it to remain relatively weak, with consumption growth moderating as well.

items.title: Municipalities await future of housing law after change in B.C. government
items.description: The B.C. Conservatives have promised to return authority to local governments to determine where housing density will go.
items._ogDesc: The B.C. Conservatives have promised to return authority to local governments to determine where housing density will go.
items.body:
Local councils returning to work in the wake of the municipal election are waiting to see what a new B.C. Conservative government does with provincial housing legislation that forced them to redo their bylaws and official community plans.

During the campaign, the party promised to return authority to local governments to determine where housing density will go.

The promise was a step back from its threat a couple of years ago to repeal Bill 44, which was enacted by the NDP government in 2023 to stimulate housing starts.

The legislation required municipalities to amend their bylaws by mid 2024 to allow four to six units on single-family and duplex lots, effectively up-zoning most of the province.

It also outlawed public hearings for development projects that conform to official community plans.

The latter raised the ire of many residents, who felt they no longer had any say on what was being built around them.

Victoria Mayor Marianne Alto, who was re-elected for a second term, said the city is waiting to see if the next government has “profoundly different directives.”

She said the 2023 provincial changes fit well with the city’s existing approach to housing development.

“Frankly our own agendas were more assertive than that anyway,” she said, adding they also didn’t have any problem with the province setting housing targets.

“We knew we’d exceed them, which we have.”

The most recent data available shows the City of Victoria had issued 2,359 occupancy permits for new homes by late fall 2025, well ahead of the goal of 1,425. Victoria’s target is to issue 4,902 occupancy permits by 2028.

Alto said the city will continue on its current path, including policies geared at producing more affordable housing, until told otherwise.

She noted that the incoming provincial government has suggested it intends to push for more affordable housing. “I suspect that they’re probably going to look at ways to do that,” she said.

Across the border in Saanich, the Bill 44 changes and loss of public hearings were a big issue for many residents.

Outgoing Saanich Mayor Dean Murdock said revising the official community plan and zoning rules to accommodate what is called small-scale multi-unit housing — like townhouses and multi-plexes — was a lot of work for district staff.

Undoing it would also require a “significant” amount of work if that’s the direction the new provincial government chooses to go, he said.

The district also created policies to guide the application process around small-scale multi-unit housing, updating its building permit language. “Those things would all have to be revised,” he said.

“This could be a major diversion in terms of priorities that a future council may set.”

Murdock said new governments are typically “allergic to the policies of their predecessors,” so while they may recognize the value in creating more family-suitable housing, they’re likely to just rip apart the current legislation.

“The issues around housing availability and affordability are not going away, and they will be very much a pressure on a Conservative government, just as it has been for an NDP government,” he said.

The Conservatives have said they will remove red tape around housing construction, review the costs that slow it down, shorten approval times and overhaul the B.C. Energy Step Code, which sets energy-efficiency requirements for new buildings.

Mike Drummond, chief executive of the Urban Development Institute, the voice of the development industry, said blanket up-zoning had unintended consequences, such as making land assembly more difficult. “In the end, we believe municipalities should have more flexibility on where added density goes.”

Drummond is also keen to see the new government tackle some of the problems stalling projects, including building code changes and permanently removing the expansion of the PST to professional services such as architectural and engineering work. The proposed expansion, which was supposed to come into effect Oct. 1, was paused by the previous NDP government

Casey Edge, executive director of the Victoria Residential Builders Association, said he would like the provincial government to limit the cost charges that municipalities can set for developers. Such charges, which are collected for water, sanitary sewers, drainage, parks and transportation upgrades to service new development, add thousands to the cost of a home, Edge said.

Last term, Victoria council considered more than doubling the fees developers pay toward infrastructure needed to support new housing, including roads, water and sewer systems, drainage and parks.

Edge said the government should also look at replacing the Step Code, enforcing interpretation of its own building code and holding municipalities accountable for permit delays.

“There should be reasonable timelines for permits,” he said. “There is no reason a permit for a new single-family home takes two weeks in one municipality and months in another municipality.”

items.title: Canadian Real Estate Correction Now Spreading To Other Provinces
items.description:
Canada’s real estate correction has largely been concentrated in one province, but that may change soon. Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA) data shows prices fell in September. All but one province moved lower, with BC going from resilient to leading the way lower in the past year. Other provinces, some of which hit record highs […]

The post Canadian Real Estate Correction Now Spreading To Other Provinces appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Canadian real estate prices fell in 8 of 9 provinces last month. Ontario and BC lead the 22.5% drop from peak, but the broader market is now sliding.
items.body:
Canada’s real estate correction has largely been concentrated in one province, but that may change soon. Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA) data shows prices fell in September. All but one province moved lower, with BC going from resilient to leading the way lower in the past year. Other provinces, some of which hit record highs in 2026, are now making sharp moves lower. An anomaly or is the rest of the market ready to correct too?

Canadian Real Estate Prices Have Dropped $189k Since Peak

Before the provincial breakdown, let’s quickly review the national data. Canadian home prices fell 0.9% (-$5,700) to $651,400 in September, 3.4% (-$22,700) lower than last year and a whopping 22.5% (-$189,000) below peak. As previously noted, the lion’s share of that downward pressure is in Ontario—and to a lesser extent, BC. However, other provinces may be ready to join the correction.

Only One Province Saw Prices Climb, Nova Scotia Abruptly Plunges

Canadian real estate prices: Monthly change in dollars, September 2026.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

Home prices only climbed in 1 of CREA’s 9 provincial indexes. The PEI benchmark rose 1.4% (+$5.1k), but that follows a 4.0% (-$15.6k) drop in August. Bucking the trend and rolling back part of the largest drop in PEI’s history are two very different stories.

The remaining 8 of 9 CREA indexes showed declines. The largest monthly decline was in Nova Scotia (-2.7%; -$11.8k), driven by an abrupt plunge in Halifax. A 1.3% (-$4.9k) drop in Saskatchewan and Ontario’s 1.0% (-$7.6k), round out the three biggest drops lower last month.

Despite the broad declines, most provinces remain higher than last year. These gains are mostly concentrated in Eastern Canada, while the Prairies were stable. Newfoundland’s 5.5% (+$18.6k) climb puts it in the lead for annual growth. It was followed by Saskatchewan, which came in 2.8% (+$10.4k) higher than last year, and New Brunswick at 2.7% (+$9.1k).

Leading the way lower over the past year is BC, where September came in 4.7% (-$42.4k) lower than last year. Ontario followed with a 3.9% (-$29.6k) drop over the same period, followed by Nova Scotia, whose monthly plunge pushed prices 2.5% (-$11.0k) lower.

Canada’s Real Estate Correction Has Only Hit 2 Provinces So Far

Decline in home prices from peak, by province.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

Not one province remains at peak, though Newfoundland is only 1.0% (-$3.7k) below its July 2026 record high. Despite peaking in the same month, PEI has plunged more than double at 2.7% (-$10.5k). Neither province is that far from the peak, and all but two provinces remain close to the record highs.

Ontario is one of those two, plunging 26.7% (-$268.8k) since its March 2022 peak. BC is a distant second, down 16.7% (-$174.3k). That massive 10-point gap highlights just how concentrated this “crash” actually is. Nova Scotia sits in third at just 4.1% (-$18.2k) below its peak. But remember, BC’s decline was in the single-digits until well into last year. Nova Scotia’s abrupt monthly plunge could mean a broader correction is just getting started.

Whether Canada’s housing slump has another leg lower is anyone’s guess. The national index is down 22.5% from peak, but only Ontario has seen a drop larger than that. It’s being called a historic, 4-year market correction—yet most provinces are still hugging their record highs. Ultimately, corrections occur to resolve market inefficiencies for buyers, not just a national model. Until regional markets make sense to local buyers, activity will remain tame.

items.title: Millennium Ups Proposed Kitsilano Rental Tower To 26 Storeys, Adding Hotel
items.description:
Vancouver-based Millennium Development has submitted a new rezoning application for their project in the Kitsilano neighbourhood of Vancouver, according to a rezoning application published by the City of Vancouver last week.

The subject site of the project is 2158-2170 W 1st Avenue, two parcels that form an internal site between Yew Street and Arbutus Street on the southern side of W 1st Avenue, a few blocks south of Kitsilano Beach.

BC Assessment records show that 2158 W 1st Avenue transacted in January 2024 for $6,000,000, while 2170 W 1st Avenue transacted in August 2024 for $22,500,000. Each parcel is occupied by an old rental building, and BC Assessment values the parcels at $2,574,000 and $11,190,000 respectively, for a total assessed value of $13,764,000 — half of the 2024 sale price.

In 2024, Millennium Development — the developer behind Olympic Village — submitted a rezoning application for a 20-storey rental tower with 185 units and 20% of the floor area provided as below-market rental. The rezoning was approved in June 2025, but the project did not advance, and Millennium — through Millennium Kitsilano Nominee Ltd. — has now submitted a new rezoning application.

2158-2170 W 1st Avenue in Vancouver. (Chris Dikeakos Architects, Millennium Development)

The site was previously rezoned from RM-4 (Residential) to CD-1 (Comprehensive Development) as part of the previous rezoning application — enacted on June 2, 2026 — and Millennium is now seeking to amend the existing CD-1 zoning to allow for a 26-storey mixed-use rental and hotel tower with a maximum height of 301 feet and a density of 8.73 FSR — up from the previous 212 ft and 6.8 FSR.

The rental component will include 121 units with a suite mix of 33 studio units, 41 one-bedroom units, 31 two-bedroom units, and 16 three-bedroom units. Of the 121 units, 97 will be market rental and 24 will be below-market rental. The units have average sizes of 415 sq. ft, 512 sq. ft, 777 sq. ft, and 1,096 sq. ft for the market rental units, while the average sizes for the below-market units are all larger.

The market rental component will be at the top of the tower and above the hotel component, which will have 99 suites from Levels 6 to 16 — 9 suites per floor. A hotel operator/brand has not been identified.

Below the hotel component will then be amenity space, followed by some additional market rental units and all of the below-market units. The ground floor of the building will include the lobby, plus 6,294 sq. ft of retail space.

Millennium says in the rezoning application that “The project does not trade housing for hotel space” and that it "delivers secured market and below-market rental housing while simultaneously addressing the City's documented hotel shortage." From the proposal, 64 rental units have been cut, and the hotel component is being added along with six additional storeys.

The site falls within the Kitsilano North - Area B sub-area of the Broadway Plan, which allows for a maximum height of 20 storeys, but Millennium cited the Vancouver Official Development Plan (ODP) — approved earlier this year — and the Residential High-Rise 1 land use designation, which allows for up to 26 storeys.

“This application is being considered under the Broadway Plan,” said the City of Vancouver in a note published alongside the rezoning application. “The application requests consideration of height and density beyond existing policy provisions and proposes a hotel use that is not contemplated under current policy.”

The rezoning application notes that “The amenity program has been expanded beyond typical residential standards (greater than 10%) to provide a broader range of spaces that support wellness, recreation, social interaction, and flexible day-to-day use for all residents,” saying that “This modest increase enhances livability without increasing residential density.”

Renderings of the proposal for 2158-2170 W 1st Avenue in Vancouver. (Chris Dikeakos Architects, Millennium Development)

Another notable change in the proposal is the addition of a third elevator, which Millennium says “ensures that daily vertical circulation meets service reliability and accessibility standards in a mixed-use building of this scale.” To accommodate the change, the tower floorplate has been increased from 6,800 sq. ft to 6,923 sq. ft.

“The proposed 6,923 sq. ft. tower floorplate is a deliberate design response that supports the long-term functionality and performance of the building,” the application notes. “The modest increase in floorplate size accommodates a third elevator, significantly improving operational resilience, reducing resident wait times, enhancing vertical transportation, enabling more efficient structural grids, improving unit layouts, and creating a cleaner architectural expression.”

Although there are now no longer minimum parking requirements, the developer is proposing to include 164 vehicle parking spaces and 339 bicycle parking spaces in a five-level underground parkade.

After publishing the rezoning application last week, the City of Vancouver is holding the Q&A period for the proposal from Wednesday, November 18 to Tuesday, December 1.
